TO tlit LARK. 0 Lark, thou dost m.y weary heart so move, Thou mak'st nvs. merry as a careless boy That plucks the gay-plumed flowers to fling again! Blest bird! the spring of thy ...,....intment show: Is it thou art to Sorrow's presence blind? Qr, being of heaven, thy music cannot cloy? Tell it to us who after solace grope. Thy art is not for solving-1 but .know Thou'rt more to tile than any of thy kind: No other songster hath such speech of hope That e'er is heard on mountain or in grove. The Nightingale sings but of earthly joy; His sweetest lays are only of his love: Bat thou hot nothing of this world's alloy; Thou tellest of the things that are above. 0 Lark, so joyous is thy simple strain, timid we but half thy music's magic prove, The secret of thy untaught rapture find, 'There worth enduring of all present pain! We idly guess: our sadness ne'er divined Thy perfect freedom fettered by no chain. Sing on, thou marvel to oar sober mind! And, singing, learn thy music is not vain, Since it cloth charm from us some thoughts of woe. Whate'er we suffer in our prison here, What sorrow, sickness, madness, or despair, Thou seem'st so blithe in thy blue realm of air, And such fell melody doth from Thee flow— The wonder is, that, having climbed so near Heaven's gate, bright songster! Thou shouldst ever care To visit us again in this-dell sphere. ..—Good words for June. CHARLES GRINDROD.

A bright-eyed boy, upon hearing his father read the story of Joan of An, was gr eatly moved by her sad trials; but I when the part was re ached Where she was about to be burned I to death at the stair() the poor little fellow could contain himself no longer, but sobbingly clutched his parent's arm, and, with big tears Tunt,ing down his plump little cheeks, I cried, "Hut, pa-pfrpa, wh-t-re were the police?" TEE -Cu OWNING- TRHASURE OF A VIETUOSO.—There -were great doings a Brentwood and in the neighbourhood lately in connection with the home coming of Mr. and Mrs. Christopher Tower after their honeymoon. Mr. and Mrs. Tower came down from London by special train, and tra- 'yelled in the Prince of Wales's saloon carriage, the use of • "which was grecionsly permitted. Brentwood railway eta- 'COß was carpeted and gaily decorated, and thousands of -people crawded tke approaches. Flowers were strewn under 'the feet of thee' happy couple," and Mrs. Tower was pre- sented with a -bouquet by a pretty little girl dressed in cream srtin: 'A procession was then formed, and moved to Weald along a triumphal way and amid repeated cheering, the playing of bands, and the ringing of church beles.e..My. Tower's speech in response to all the compli- raentethateetere paid him was a chivalrous one. "It has long been a joke against me," he remarked in one portion of it, " that I never return home without bringing with use soideTresb. .erticle of tirtu to add to my collection at the old home. I think, however, you will agree with me that I must now draw a line at the foot of the catalogue, as I flatter myself Itave to-day brought home the finest and most sterling-treasure that can be found." Weald Hall, it may be added; is an interesting old house, situated in a noble park, and commanding extensive views of some of the prettiest and most undulating country in Essex. It has long been the family seat of the Towers. When the present occupant entered into possession, he had the walls cleared of paper and plaster, and discovered, in many rooms, fine oak panels, running from door to ceiling. In one room a magnificent mural painting was also found above the mantel- piece, and this is now protected by an oaken screen. Rich Saud rare gems crowd every corner, Mr. Tower being a vir- tuoso. Especially noticeable are the tapistry and pictures, these latter including some fine landscapes by Landseer. Mr. Tower is an excellent landlord, and the homesteads and cottages on his estate are among the best in the country.— !Law/. Aw Aterretel• Picreene—The trees are not yet leafless, but look thin, and allow us to discover all sorts of secrets. -Here is the nest of the blackbird that sang so deliciously in the summer evening; and here the home of the thrush who, undaunted by the cold, ungenial summer, chanted his matins all the louder because the rain fell fast. Close by, now, the winter robin carols, while above his head the small colony of rooks that have their spring and summer residence in the beechee, are wheeling solemnly to and fro,' as if some one of their number was drilling them previous to , their migrating for the winter to one of the larger companies' in a park near by ; while, as the Vicar paces to and fro on the moss walk by the north wall, conning his sermon for to- morrow, we note that from time to time he raises his hand to brush away a line Of cobweb that, hung with mist-drops, glitters every now and then in the sunshine like a tiny chain of diamonds. On the south wall a late peach glows, and golden-drop plums hang enticingly against the grey wall; 'while, under the west wall, the newly robbed bees lazily boom round a hive that, turned on its side and filled with refuse honey, is to feed them and compensate them for the , golden store that has just been taken away from them. It is most interesting to watch, even with an eye uneducated in their mysteries, how regular, how' wonderful, are the habits of these tiny creatures should a strange bee venture Dear the hive, in one second he is attacked and either killed or else so maltreated that he soon learns the old lesson that honesty is the best policy. Wasps and drones are treated -similarly, and if a bee should die his body is at once turned outof the hive and dropped swiftly on the ground. The bees soon notice we are strangers, and detaching a scout from their number, send him buzzing round us in such a sugges- tive manner that we perforce retire lest a worse thing should happen to us.—" Pictures of Rural Life," in Good Words. Aer IMMENSE VESSEL, 2,100 YEARS AGO.—The most prodigious vessel on the records of the ancients was built by order of hero, the second Tyrant of Syracuse, under the superintendence of Archimedes, about 230 years before Christ, the description of which would fill a small volume. Athenteua has left a description of this vast floating fabric. There was, he states, as much timber employed in her as would have served for the construction of fifty galleys. It •had all thewarieties of apartments and conveniences neces- sary to a palace—such as banqueting-rooms, baths, a library, temple of Venus, gardens, fish-ponds, mills and a spacious' gymnasium. The inlaying of the floors of the middle apart- ment represented in various colours the stories of Homer's "Iliad ;" there were everywhere the most beautiful paintings, And every embellishment and ornament that art could fur- enish were bestowed on the ceilings, windows, and every part. eThe inside of the temple was inlaid with cypress-wood, the -statutes were of ivory, and the floor was studded with ,precious stones. This vessel had twenty benches of oars, And was encompassed by an iron rampart or battery; it had also eight towers with walls and bulwark, which were fur- nished with machines of war, one of which was capable of • throwing a stone of 300 pounds weight, or a dart of twelve cabitolong to the distance of half a mile. To launch her, Archimedes invented a screw of great -power. She had four wooden and eight iron anchors; her mainmast, com- posed of a single tree, was procured after much trouble from distant inland mountains. Hiero finding that he had no harbours in Sicily capable of containing her, and learning that there was famine in Egypt, sent her loaded with corn to Alexandria. She bore an inscription of which the follow- ing is part :—"Hiero, the son of Hieroclesethe Dorian, who wields the sceptre of Sicily, -sends this vessel bearing in her .the fruits of The earth. Do thou, 0 Neptune preserve in -safety this ship over the blue waves."—" The Sea: its Stir- ling Story of A dventure, Peril and Heroism." Pikratnio AtLIGATORS.—The alligator-fisher finds his most remunerative business in the capture of newly-hatched, orerather, still juvenile, reptiles. Great is the excitement when the discovers.a nice little nursery party of about fifty scaly babies, front eix inches to a foot in length, all basking in some shallow, seemly pool. Though sharp-toothed from their birdie they cats be handled without danger, if only he can elude the vigilanee of their keen-eyed old mother, who is basking on the shore, or else buried in the mud, witlfonly her eyes and nostrils in sight. (All the saurian species alike have the eyes And noetrila so raised above any other part of the head, that they can Lie buried in the mee, observinga their neighbours, without any fear of detection or exposing ay vital part to the danger a a shot.) Baby alligators of about ,twelve inches in length, when captured and brought to market, are bought by devisers and prices ranging frem two to tour dollars a dozen. The retail price is ranch higher, as it is-very difficult to rear the creatures in captivity. In the case of larger individual specimens, the tislaers receive an additional sum of from fifty coats to a dollar for each foot above a certain length. It bacrecently occurred to the great American mind that, since these reptiles are now a re- cognised article of trade with a deficite market value, it may pay to rear these as well as any other species of stock; and moreover, that the muddy shores of many a stagnant pool in the Southern States' which hitherto have been acl counted worm than useless breeding only feeers and pestici lential miasmas beneath the blazing pun, way leew be turne to account, and indeed become valuable propert7,—Caseell's Family Magazine.

In the case referred to, the Land Commissioners fixed the tenant right at £7OO, but in the market the hold- ing brought £l,lBO. The returns apply to 82 tenancies. The total area of the holdings extends to about 4.338 sta- tute a-jres, the annual rental is £3,645, or about Hs. 10d. per acre. *-The total sum paid for the "tenancies," that is the tenants' interests in the holdings, was £35,624, being an average of £8 4s. 2d. per acre. CHESHIRE BRANCH OF THE FARMERS' ALLIANCE.

div.head: MR. LATHAM ON THE AGRICULTURAL HOLDINGS
div.p: MR. LATHAM ON THE AGRICULTURAL HOLDINGS
BILL.

A meeting of the Cheshire branch .of the Farmers' Alliance was held on Saturday, in the Assatnbly-rootn of the Golden Lion Inn, Ches'er, for the purpose of discussing am, ndments considered necessary in the Agricultural Hold- ings Bill. The chair was occupied by Mr. G. W. Lltham, the president of the branch, and there was a fair attend- ance.

The Cruntrame, in opening the proceedings, expressed his regret that no deputation from the Farmers' Alliance had been able to attend. Mr. Borlase, M.P., the president, had informed him about three weeks ago that he had arranged that a deputation should come, but he had since received a letter from the secretary to the Alliance stating that the deputation could not be present, and the members of Parliament could not possibly leave London at this moment. Mr. Latham then suggested that they should discuss the bill as amended by the committee of the Alliance, and let Mr. Borlase, M.P., know what clauses they wished to see amended. They had all been very anxious to see protection given to the sitting tenant, and they had already expressed the opinion that, however necessary it was to protect the out- going ren.int, the bulk of the tenants and the best of them were sitting tenante, and they, a fortiori, ought to be pro- tected. But after the way in which Mr. Shaw-Lefevre, who was practically the mouth-piece of the Government, spoke on the second reading of the bill in the House of Commons, he (Mr. Litham) was perfectly hopeless that they would be able to secure that protection thoroughly and directly in any bill that could be carried in the present Parliament. The Alliance in clause 7 proposed to get over • the difficulty by introducing an amerdment to the effect that when notice was given by a landlord to his tenant of his intention to raise the rent on his holding, they should go to arbitration at once. But as long as they gave a landlord power to evict when a tenant did not pay the rent that the landlord chose to fix, he (Mr. Latham) held that all that arbitration was practically worthless. Having referred to the case of a tenant who laid out enough of money to make his com- pensation worth £1,500, and who felt that he was safe for life, as his landlord, being needy, could never repay that amount, and was not likely to get a tenant A% would pay it, Mr. Latham said it might-be that there were hindrances to a landlord raising his rent, but he did not think that in the case alluded to the man was at all safe. If there was an eagerness to take farms, as there was some twelve or fourteen years ago, did they not think that for that im- proved farm the landlord might find plenty of people to pay compensation, and to pay him higher rent too, the higher rent being paid, not for the value of the manures, but for the cleanliness of the farm and the good condition into which it was brought? He believed that they never could make a man safe merely by paying him for his improve- ments. What they must get was a judicial rent; they muet get some power by which a court could settle what was a fair rent between man and bran, and enact that as long as a tenant paid that rent he should not be disturbed. Until they got that they were at the mercy of every landlord who chose or was fool enough to evict an improving tenant. Still they would not get it yet. He was afraid they were farther off a judi- cial rent than ever, in consequence of what had happened in Ireland. But they might depend upon it that when people came to their senses, and when they saw that under the judicial rents Ireland was flourishing—as it would flourish by-and-bye--then Parliament would be much more disposed than it was to have the system of judicial rents that they had got in Ireland introduced into this country too, and the English tenant farmers would have justice done them. What he recommended the farmers to do was to accept the bill as a stepping-stone to something better. (Applause.) It would be a perfect act of madness to throw it out. There were two grand principles enunciated in the bill : the first, that a man should be paid for the actual im- provement he had made on the farm; and the second, that the claim for improvements, if they were still in existence, would not be invalidated by any limit of time. They must not reject those two principles because they could not get as much as they wished in the rest of the bill. Like those who engaged in a game of chess, they should be content with a move at a time, keeping their ground and getting gradually nearer the end they had in view, and in this way they would win at last. (Applause.) Mr. Latham went on to say it was suggested that there should be no schedules at all, and that the following words should be introduced in the eighth section:—"lmeirovement means any work or operation exe- cuted by a tenant upon the holding which adds to its let- ting value as a farm." It was proposed that no consent of the landlord, no trouble in giving the landlord notice, or anything of that sort should be required, but that if the ar- bitrators said that a man, with or without the consent of his landlord, had improved his land so as to make the farm worth more as a farm than it had been worth, he should be paid for his work. There was only one exception to that, and that was that the landlord's consent should be obtained to the erection or enlargement of buildings. Mr. BAXTER said the bill did not at all come up to his expectations, but he advised the tenant farmers to accept it. If it was thought necessary an agitation for further agrarian legislation could afterwards be commenced. He proposed that the bill be amended so as to ensure compensa- tion to a tenant on quitting his holding at the determination of a tenancy, "or on entering into a fresh contract of tenancy." Those few words would supply a great want in the bill.

The proposition was accepted by the meeting. Mr. LATHAM said it was suggested as a further amend- ment to the bill, "That any agreement manifestly contrary to or illusory of the intent of the Act shall be null and void." He remarked that unless some such clause were inserted in the bill it would not be worth the paper it was printed on. A motion in favour of this amendment in the bill was adopted. A resolution in favour of one year's notice to quit being made compulsory was also carried. A long discussion took place on a motion to the effect that the law of distress should be entirely abolished by the new measure, Mr. Holland, Mr. Lathatn, and Mr. Davidson pointing out that that law had caused rents to be raised, led to the acceptance by landlords of tenants who were merely men of straw, and inflicted other hardships On farmers. Mr. Minshull, on the other hand, contended that the law was a source of protection and oftentimes of assistance to poor hardworking tenants. The motion in favour of the total abolition of the law of distress, on being put to the meeting, was carried by a largo majority. It was also agreed that it was advisable to introduce into the 2Sth section the words, "Improvement means any work or operation executed by a tenant upon the holding which adds to its letting value as a farm," and to abolish the schedules, the consent of the land- lord not to be required except in the case of erection or en- largement of buildings. A resolution was likewise adopted in favour of the tenant being helped by arbitration taking place in the case of a rise of rent.

div.head: PRINTER'S DEVIL-v.
div.p: THE PRINTER'S DEVIL-v.

[By Aeroto-Scorus.] We have lost to America—for a time at least—the services of the very tall and good-natured son of the "warm land," who not so very long ago "backed the winner," and spent a portion of the proceeds of his so doing in a trip to Ireland. While there he walked twelve miles on purpose to cut a walking-stick for me out of a plantation wherein grows " wood that bugs or insects of any kind won't touch." He also took some trouble in getting for ins a bottle of private-still whisky." But his relations with the Printer's Devil had been of such a peculiar nature, that I was not at all surprised when, on his return to England, he informed me that the stick and the whisky were all right up to the time when he took the train at Holyhead for London, but that both must have been spirited away from him at a " statioa where he got out of the railway carriage to get a cup of co:fee." His latest Caxtonian exploit before depart- ing for America was to render " 0 tempora, 0' mores," into "The temper of Moses." I don't know that he has left any of his entire suits of clothes behimi him, and I don't think any of the 'ship could wear any one of his garments with comfort or convenience, but one individual member has, I am afraid, got hold of one of his old braces, or a garter, or possibly it may be a bauchle. At all events, hie " middle- parting" or mental judgment the other day got either touzzled or fogged. In a leading paragraph he had to set up for a service newspaper, commenting on the fact of the abolition of the rank and functions of the regimental sergeant instructor of musketry not being a step in the right direction towards army reform, occurred the following sentence :—"The result of this persistent endeavour to make of the ordinary serjeant a sort of Admirable Crichton is that, when the time arrives, when a clear head is neces- sary, the unfortunate non-commissioned officer can only remember a mass of things, but nothing distinctly.' " Un- like the "unfortunate non-corn." alluded to, the compositor evidently neither remembered the combined recerd of cele- brated individuals who have figured in history or literature in connection with the title of "Admirable," nor one of them in particular. The history of Aben-Esra, the Spanish rabbin born at Toledo, was a sealed book to him; and heaven only knows what he would have said had the person who dealt out the copy told him that the Jas. Crichton whom Roger B icoa called "The Admirable Doctor," was a Scotch- man! His metaphorical ideas for the time were of the hybrid order, and so he interpreted the writer's meaning in a kind of horse-marine fashion. He first of all set up " Admiral Crichton," and then coolly set about altering the copy to suit his view of the case. Neither reading-boy, reader, nor the person who gave out the copy could move him from his opinion; nor would I be surprised, if he should have the pleasure, or otherwise, of reading these lines, if he still insists that "admiral "is the word, net "admirable!' To those readers of The Examiner—if any there be of that opinion— who think I have devoted too much space to this incident, I must excuse myself on the ground that I should like these articles to be as instructive to young printers as they may be interesting or amusing to older ones. A reference to a " Reader's handbook " would have cleared the difficulty. The printer is not the only artisan who too often sets about his work with an insufficient numb!r of tools. To resume, perhaps some of those individuals who are no sooner admitted mem- bers of the so-called society of " Correctors of the Press," than they put the letters " C.P." after their names on their business cards, can tell ma what the following (cut from the Morning Post of Thursday. May 24th) meattn:—

ripHE RTDE, Hyde-park.—Day and night, in carriages JL and In cabs, at full speed, some ladies have for a long time followed a punter named have followed him to his lodging in liegent-square, and have forowed him to his workial.ce in Exeter-street, dtrand, but Vie ladies have not been able to wait. Being lame and short- sighted, the printer claims as an invalid, privilege against etiquette. The clergy say that in such a case privilege wou.d be allowed against the printed etiquette for the mart iige ser- vice. If one of the ladies makes the printer's arquaintance, and a satisfactory explanation is not given, the lady's father, mo her, brothers, and her other relatives, except her sisters, will be forbidden to make the printer's acquaintance until the expiration of 21 years.

I will not comment upon the folly of ladies following printers, nor dilate upon the wonderful feat of a lame and short-sighted man being able to outstrip and get away from the wiles of the female occupants of carriages and cabs drawn by horses galloping at full speed. I will merely say that the office of the Morning Post is situated nearly op- posite Exeter-street, and that the Printer's Devil alone, of all members of the 'ship, could have succeeded in getting it asserted in print, in that journal above all others, that a vehicle of any kind could, at the present day, pass at full speed through Exeter-street. The 'ship of the Morning Post at least ought to have known better, seeing that not long ago a worthy and respected member of their literary staff (whose neatness and taste in dress are as commendable as are the diction and scholarship of his writings) found great difficulties in threading his way on foot through the narrow street in question. No sooner had he cleared the crowd who were listening to the vocalisation of the ft male who elects now and then to bathe in the Serpentine with members of the opposite sex, than he had to run.the gauntlet of the carrier boys for the stores, who sling about in a play- ful manner from one to the other the smaller parcels in the act of loading. Trying to save his hat, he cannoned against a packing-case, tearing his coat in an ugly manner. No sooner had he escaped Scylla in this shape than he was confronted with Charybdis, in the person of a printer's devil, who very nearly succeeded in douching him with carbolic acid. The personal appearance of the genial and kind-hearted individual alluded to was a short time ago satirically described in some verses, entitled " First Nigbters." But "(lately D—, dawdling to his stall" in a London theatre to witness the first performance of a new play, in a torn coat, and his other clothing reeking with the fumes of a couple of quarts of carbolic acid, would indeed be a sight to see and remember. A cab or carriage go at full speed through Exeter-street ! Why, even Queen Elizabeth had to stoop her head in pass- ing through the doorway of a room in the great Lord Burghley' house which stood on the site, and from which the street takes its name ! And although it is on record that Dr. Johnson wrote his tragedy of " Irene in the garret of the house at one time occupied by Norris, the stayinaker ; be --no, never mind the expletive— if he could do so now (supposing him to be alive) with the Salvation Army at one end of the street, and half-a-dozen bands composed of the boy members from as many philan- thropic societies, all braying forth and drumming away at the same time at the other end. He would be more likely to commit atragedy, or ask the staymaker to make him a straight-waistcoat. The jehu and his steeds would indeed be flversthat could dash at full speed through Exeter- street. In this case the Printer's Devil has certainly "scored one "against the newspaper.

div.head: THRILLING BALLOON STORY.
div.p: A THRILLING BALLOON STORY.

1 A special correspondent has interviewed M. L'Hoste, the intrepid aeronaut who attempted to cross the Cinema on Friday night last in the balloon Pilastre de Rosier, and was picked up in the North Sea on Saturday evening by a French luvver, bound for Antwerp. M. L'Hoste describes passing the first night in the midst of a fog, and descending at Dunkirk. Being determined to persevere, he calmly took breakfast in his car, surrounded by a gaping crowd, and afterwards increased his score of ballast. Noticing a favour- able change in the wind, he ungrappled, and rose gradually to a height of 5,000 meters. He must have travelled quickly, for he soon found himself over the sea, off the coast of Belgium. Far up amongst the clouds he found a terrible difference in the weather, for, almost without warning, he sailed into a violent storm-wave. Here the beating of the rain, the heavy gusts of wind, and the loud reverberation of the thunder put the stability of the balloon ,to a fearful and unforeseen test. The whole fabric was con- vulsed with continuous vibration, and tossed and pitched in a manner which made it difficult for the giddy and be- numbed aeronaut to keep his hold on the car. However, with some difficulty he managed to open the valve, and descended at noon on Saturday to within, as far as he could calculate, eight hundred metres of the sea. Unfortunately, in the lower strata there prevailed a thick fog, which made I it impossible for him to ascertain his exact whereabouts. I He maKle another ascent in hopes of finding the elements more propitious, but the storm was still raging up in the clouds, and he therefore considered it prudent to keep nearer the sea. As the afternoon wore on he noticed with alarm that the gas in his balloon was dangerously decreasing, and he began to realise his peril. At tour o'clock the ropes dang- ling from the car touched the sea, and he knew that the critical time had come. The whole of his ballast, of which the car could hold but a comparatively limited supply, had by this time become completely exhausted, He at once threw out, one after another instruments, cases, and indeed every movable article in the car. But the balloon reapon led languidly, and in a very few minutes the car itself touched the water, and the sea broke furiously almost every minute clean over the car, drenching its unhappy occupant to the skin. The ropes and lines, too, were dashed about in a bewildering manner, and these combined horrors had almost made M. L'Hoste despair, when he caught sight of the sails of a fish- ing lugger, which turned out to be the Noemi. The cap- tain of the Noemi almost simultaneously caught sight of the balloon, which he for some time took to be a ship on fire, and manoeuvred round and round accordingly. When, however, be ascertained what the strange craft really was, he launched a boat, and with immense difficulty rescued the aeronaut from a fate which, but for his timely appear- ance, would not long have been delayed. L'Hoste found he had, been rescued within ten miles of the English coast. He and the balloon, which had burst, were taken aboard the Noemi and landed at Antwerp shortly after midnight, L'Hoste is full of gratitude to the captain of the Noemi.

Mr. Daniel, Q.C., Judge of the Leeds County Court, has drawn the attention of the solicitors practising before him to a statement attributed to Mr. Chamberlain, M.P.,namely, " that the great majority of trustees appointed heretofore were little better than swindlers." The learned Jadge said that the statement, so far as the three important courts over which he presides were concerned, was a calumnious libel. At Leicester, two teen have, been sent for trial for conspiring to defraud creditorh by making fictitious claims in liquid- ating estates—an offence which it is believed to be of fre- quent occurrence, and by no means confined to persons in a " small way " of business.

div.p: MISCELLAND)US.

In the international chess tournament at the Criterion, London, on Monday afternoon, Zukertort beat Blackburne, and thus won the first prize of £3OO. Mr. Althrman Roe (Liberal) was the only candidate nomi- nated for the vacincy at Derby on Monday, and he was accordingly declared duly elected. The tenour of the crop reports is that everything is making good progress, excepting grass, which is light as a rule, and that a soaking rainfall is now the one thing needful. The Gaiety Theatre of Varieties, situate in. Peter-street, Manchester, was destroyed by fire on Saturday. It is not known how the fife broke out. At Drimpton, a Dorset village, 21 cottagers have been rendered homeless by a disastrous fire which broke out there, doing great damage to property. The Guardians of the Stratford-on-Avon Union, which comprises 37 parishes, have decided to adopt the Berk- shire system of relieving tramps which provides relief stations in all villages, where wayfarers may obtain a mid- day meal. Thomas Moorland and Thomas M•Aline, two railway workers, were killed on the Union line, at Glasgow, on Mon- day. While engaged working at a bridge a train came upon them unawares, and both men were knocked down and killed. They were aged 26 and 24. ENGLISH Couarry COURTS.—A parliamentary return shows that the number of plaints entered in the county courts of England and Wales daring 1882 was 1,009,185 for sums not exceeding aO. 11.771 for sums above £2O and not exceed- ing £5O, and 270 for sums above £5O. Of all the cases determined, only 9880 were in favour of the defendant. COLLIERY EXPLOSION.—On Sunday night a serious col- liery explosion occurred at Brinsley fit, near Nottingham, owned by Messrs. Barber, Walker, and Co. Two hostlers, nanaed Wright and Dunn, had descended to perform their dnties, when tbe explosion occurred, and both sustained frightful injuries. It is feared Wright cannot recover. Fourteen valuable horses were killed; and had the explo- sion occurred when the miners were at work, the conse- quences must have been disastrous. THE NEW LIVERPOOL Kattozer.—Mr. W. B. Forwood, of Liverpool, has accepted the offer of knighthood made to him by the Premier in commemoration of the opening of the new North Docks in September, 1881, by the Prince and Princess of Wales, during which time Mr. Forwood was Mayor of Liverpool, and took a prdminent part in the pro- ceedings. A baronetcy, it is understood, was offered to Mr. T. D. Hornby, chairman of the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board, but that gentleman has declined the honour. There is now abundant evidence that the Billingsgate " ring" has been effectually broken, and London working Men are rejoicing in a plentiful supolv of cheap fish. During the last few days there has been an extraordinary demand for all kinds of fish at the Central Market, Smith- field, and it is stated that although the supply was very large, twice the quantity on offer could readily have been soli% It is now possible to buy, retail, salmon at L 3 to la 4d per lb, soles at 9d per lb, turbot at 7d per /la, and other kinds of fish v,equally reasonable prices. CYCLISTS' MEET AT Livuurocm.—The seventh annual, " monstre meet" of cyclists took place at Sefton Park, Liverpool, on Saturday, in delightful weather, and attracted ft large attendance both of cyclists and of spectators. Fifty- two bicycle and tricycle clubs were represented, besides un- attached riders. Amongst the towns at a distance which sent representatives were Manchester, Stretford, Chester, Clitheroe, Huddersfield, Accrington, Blackburn, Mold, Horn- Se!, Chesterfield, Wigan, and Sheffield. After a parade round the park the meet was photographed. A tug of war took place afterwards between various clubs. THE MALAGASY ENVOYS AND ENGLISH ADVICE.—A French newspaper credits Lord Granville with baying given excellent, though it may be unpalatable, advice to the Malagasy Envoys. The Foreign Secretary is reported to to have told them that no European Power will interfere in their behalf in their quarrel with France, and as that coun- try must triumph sooner or later, their wisest course is to accept the French terms now, instead of hereafter subjecting themselves to others that would he more onerous. Whether Lord Granville has held this language to the Envoys or not, its truth is unquestionable, and if peace be thus brought about, his lordship's intervention will be appreciated in Paris.

Lord Coleridge's summing up in the recent case of "Regina v. Foote and others" for blasphemous libel has Just been published. His Lordship has written a brief pre- fee!, in which he explains that the charge is published as he has been told that a correct version of it may be useful, though it must not be considered as put forward by him With any pretension to its being a complete or exhaustive discussion of the question. No one, he says, can be more Sensible than himself of its shortcomings; he did not, he confesses, appreciate the importance of the occasion, and he Was not at the moment capable of any careful or sustained effort. He did not conceive that he was doing more than discharging a common ditty in a common manner. Mn. CRApLIN, M.P., AND RADICALISM —The members of lhe Hull Radical Club having passed a resolution express- mg their satisfaction that Mr. Chaplin recently opposed Perpetual pensions, and having congratulated him upon entering upon the path of Radical reform, Mr. Chaplin's secretary has replied as follows :—" I am requested by Mr. Chaplin to acknowledge with thanks the kindly expression A)f opinion which you have sent him on behalf of the Radi- al Club, but Mr. Chaplin must demur to the last para- graph of the resolution, and would regret to receive a vote of thanks under false pretences, for he cannot acknowledge that reform of abuses or anomalies is a distinctive feature of Radicalism, or can be claimed by that party alone." MESSRS. CASSELL, PETTER, AND GALPIN are entitled to the credit of being the first firm in London to carry out the system of co-operative industry in its full development. There are one or two firms in which the principle is applied in a limited sense, but Messrs. Cassell have turned their firm into a limited company, with a view to enable all their employes to participate in the partnership.. Mr. Forster Presided at a tea given by the heads of the firm to their Workmen at Exeter Hall, on Saturday night, to celebrate this important change, and announced that he had himself be- come a shareholder in the company. Shares to the amount of £lO,OOO have been taken by 300 employes, who are each to pay an instalment of is. per week. THE IMPRISONMENT OF MESSRS FOOTE AND RAMSAY. --11Ve (Daily News) understand that two additional Memorials have just been sent in to the Home Secretary Praying for the remission of the senitiences imposed on ,Messrs. Foote and Ramsay for blasphemy. One of these oears the signatures of a large body of Cambridge graduates and undergraduates, including some of the most distin- guished fellows and lecturers. The other is signed by a number of Scotch professors, including several professors Of divinity and moral philosophy. Among other influen- tial names we notice those of Principal Caird and Pro- 25sor Ed. Caird, of Glasgow, Professors Fraser and David alasson, of Edinburgh, and Professor T. Spencer Baynes, of st. Andrews. TEE NEWSPAPER PRESS Fume —The Newspaper Press sund. which was established over 20 years ago, continues to grow in membership, influence, and importance. On Saturday night the annual dinner was held in Willis's- reams, under the presidency of the Right Hon. Mr. Childers, 'l•Pe Chancellor of the Exchequer, and proved in every wav successful. Speaking of the development of the news- Paper Press, the chairman said its functions seemed to be not so much to give ,indieficinal opinions upon a perticular cluster of events as to focus together the whole mass of 46718, so that public men might be enabled to learn the cur- rent of'events in all parts of the world. Amongst the speakeee Were Lord Houghton (the president of the fund), Lord (erard, Sir Lepel Griffin, and the Madagascar Ambissador. 831 ir Julius Benedict conducted the musical programme at the banquet. COLLISION IN THE CHANNEL —Early on Saturday morn- mg the London, Chatham, and Dover Company's steamer Wave, carrying the mails from Paris, was run into by the • ranch barque Fanny, several passengers on the steamer be- littg seriously injured and one killed. The morning was es"gger, and the steamer was apparently proceeding on its course, at its usual spe'd, and taking the usual pre- cautions. The steamer, on which' there were 101 passengers, 17,a8 40 minutes out from Calais at the time of the collision. the barque escaped with comparatively slight injury, but Wave had her starboard paddle box and starboard stan- eauicns damaged, and the aft funnel and mainmast carried erV• One of the passengers, Mr. E. L. Barnett, a jeweller, `B't !iirmingham, was killed by a portion of the mainmast i'hing him on the head and fracturing his skull. A penny laid out at compuncr, interest at the birth of our Saviour would in the year 1775 have amounted to a solid mass of gold 1,800 times the weight of the whole globe. Mr. Errington, M.P., who left Rome for England on Sun- day night, has, it is said, declined an invitation to address his constituents on the subject of his mission to the Vatican. The model for a bronze statue of Lord Frederick Caven- dish, which is ta ba placed in front of the new Town Hall in Barrow-in-Furness, has been finished by the sculptor, Mr. Bruce Joy. The cotton-waste warehouse of W. and L. Smithies, Saville-street, Bolton, caught fire on Wednesday night. The fire spread rapidly from end to end, but was got under in about an hour after the roof had fallen in. The damage is about £4,000, which is partially covered by insurance. THE SAVINGS OF A" KNOOKER-UP."—An inquest has been held in Wigan on the body of an old man named John Higham, a "knocker-up," who had lived by himself for ever twenty years, and who was found dead in bed. On searching the house the friends of the deceased found £92 in one of the drawers. The explosion of a boiler at'a paper works near Barnsley, whereby two men, named Norman and Porteus were killed, was further investigated by the district coroner on Tuesday. It was shown that leakage of water from a valve which the stoker could not see caused the explosion, and a verdict of accidental death was returned. ASSIZE BUSINESS.—We understand that we are about to see an innovation in regard to the assize business of the Northern Circuit, inasmuch as civil cases as well as criminal will be taken in Manchister and Liverpool at the autumn assizes to be held in October and November. Heretofore there has been criminal business only at these assizes. On Wednesday morning, a well-dressed man, of about 40 years of age, was seen to mount the parapet of Blackfriars Bridge, and before the passers-by bad time to save him, leaped into the Thames and immediately sank. A boat was put off from Blackfriars Pier, but the man never rose. He is stated to have been of full stature, with slight whiskers, and to have carried a small hand bag. A man named John Walton has just been found dead at Leicester on his doorstep. The deceased had been drinking heavily, and it is supposed that being unable to open the door he sat down and expired. When discovered he had the keys in his hands and a cigar in his mouth. Death is at- tributed to heart disease. Some months ago the Great Western Railway Company decided to close their extensive engine works at Stafford- road, Wolverhampton, on the Friday evening in each week until Monday morning, thus reducing the working time of the men by about five and a quarter hours per week. It is now announced that the works are again to be opened on Saturdays as before, commencing with the present week. `1 he works employ about one thousand pairs of hands. Intelligence received from Lloyd's states that the steamer Joseph Dodds, of Newcastle, 1,058 tons register, homeward bound from the Black Sea to England with a full cargo ot grain, valued at £15,000, struck on a sunken rock about 40 miles from the Dog Rock Lighthouse, on the African coast, and almost immediately foundered. The crew escaped in the boats, but the captain, who went down into the cabin for the ship's papers, was drowned. The general committee of the Scottish Liberal Club, Edinburgh, have adopted a resolution sympathising with the motives which induced Lord Rosebery to resign the Under-Secretaryship of the Home Office, expressing their regret at his severance from public, and particularly Scottish affairs, and recording their high sense of his ser- vices, and trusting he may soon be placed in such an official position as will enable him to render further benefits to the country. At the Manchester City Sessions, on Thursday morning, Joe Toner and John Warren, tbe two men who broke into the shop of Mr. M. Beaver, jeweller. Cross-street, and at- tempted to open a tale containing a very large quantity of diamonds and jewellery, were brought up for trial. They pleaded guilty, and it was urged on their behalf that they were not armed and did not make any resistance when arrested. The Recorder said he took into consideration the fact that they were not armed and did not resist the police, and sentenced each to five years' penal servitude. DARING ESCAPR OF A FRIsONER.—On Thursday, a pri- soner named William Roach, who was waiting trial at Cardiff on charges of housebreaking, escaped from his cell in the dinner hour, and got through a hole in the wall of the jail, where, at some height above the ground, sanitary alterations are in progress, and descended, removed the ladder from the scaffolding to the boundary wall, and sprang over. Next, he hid himself among the tombstones in the old cemetery which is near, hut, on being observed, scaled the wall and ran down some bye streets, where he was ultimately captured by Warder Ross, after a smart chase. FOIINDERING OF A NEVir YORK STEAMER: FIFTY LIVES LOST.—lnformation received from Lloyd s states that all hopes have been given up respecting the safety of the fine iron steamer Africa, 1495 tons register, which sailed from New York fcr Leith two months since with a full cargo of flour, cheese, bacon, and ether produce valued at £30,000. Underwriters are of opinion that the vessel must have been sunk by ice, as no trace whatever has been found of the mis- sing ship. Her crew numbered 50 men all told, and it is feared that they have perished, as nothing has been heard as

to their fate. At the London Bankruptcy Court, on Thursday, an ap- plication was made to Mr. Registrar Razlitt to register the resolutions passed by the creditors under this liquidation. The petition was presented a short time since, the debtor describing himself as of 17, Abbey- road, St. John Wood. The accounts produced at the meeting showed debts unsecured £435,416, debts fully secured £2OO, and assets £39,131, including an item of surplus from securities to the amount of £3,553. Resolutions were passed providing for the liquidation of the estate by arrangement, with Mr. Luke Bishop, aecoentant, as trustee, with a committee of inspection. Upon the applies- _ .

tion of Mr. W. H. Roberts regsitration was ordered. ATTEMPTED FRAUDS ON THE HOSPITAL SUNDAY FUNDS. —A painful circumstance in connection with the London Hospital Sunday Fund collection is an attempted fraud by persons who have issued a circular to various churches in Lambeth and elsewhere, stating that collectors would be sent to receive Hospital Sunday money. The secretary of the fund, Mr. Henry N. Custance, repudiates this document, which he describes as a forgery; and he cautions the metro- politan congregations not to part with their money save to the authorities at the Mansion House. The intimation of the fraud was first received by the secretary of the fund from the Upton Baptist Chapel, and a copy of the circular was immediately despatched. to the head offices of the Metropolitan and City Police. The report ad interim of the Welsh Congregational fund has just been published, and contains a tabulated statement showing the amount collected by each Union towards liquidating the chapel debts. In Cardiganshire the aronunt of debt owing at March, 1882, was £3,076, and the amount paid up during the year ended March, 1883, was £363; Northern Carnarvonshire, debt £16,253, paid up £1,088; Western Carnarvonshire, £12,499, paid up £953; Denbigh- shire and Flintshire (incomplete return), £9,262, paid up £315; Merionethshire, £9.607, paid up £617; Montgomery- shire. £9,607, paid up £617 ; Montgomeryshire, £1,780, paid up £315. The total debt was £182002, and the amount p,aid up £20,283, so that more than £20,000 has been paid during the year ending March, 1883, towards liquidating the debts resting on the Congregational chapels in Wales. United Ireland says :—While Mr. Sexton was denouncing in the House of Commons the judicial mtirder of Suleiman Sarni, and telling the Ministry that all the water in the ocean could not wash from them his blood, Mr. Wilson, the member for Middlesborough, who was sitting on the cross bench close to Mr. Callan, cried in a voiceloud enough to be heard by his neighbours, though not by the House, "All the water in the ocean would not wash away the blood of Lord Frederick Cavendish away from you. You miserable ruffian." Mr. Callan whispered in his ear, "If you said that outside the House I'd pull your nose." United Ireland says the Irish electors of Middlesborough will have an op- portunity soon of pulling Mr. Wilson's nose in a metaphori- cal but painful sense in the balloting booth, and drive him to the necessity of expressing his sentiments outside the House hereafter. A PEER IN THE COUNTY COURT.—Lord Aylesford was On

Wednesday summoned to the Bloomsbury County Court by Mr. Russell, proprietor of the Lotus Club, for £54 Sc., money lent. The defendant had paid £l9 111. into court. Mr. Thomas France, steward, said that in the year 1881 the defendant barrowed several sums of money. On a Sunday evening in December the defendant had a large dinner party, and borrowed £24 us. 6d., and on another occasion he borrowed £lO, promising to send a cheque for the amount by eleven o'clock on the following day. He had asked the defendant on several occasions for the money, and had been to his chambers in Chapel-street, but was unable to see him. Mr. Lyon, counsel for the defendant, stated that his lordship was- unable to be present that day, but after the evidence that had been given he weald consent to a verdict for the amount claimed. THE DEMASTDEOR LABOUR 1N THE ENGINEERING tRADES —The returns just issued by the trades union societies con- nected with the engineering branches of industry show a slight falling off,in the demand for labour. The increase of unemployed members is not such as to represent any serious falling off in the activity of trade, but there is evi- dently a less pressing demand for skilled labour in some branches, which would seem to indicate a check in the un- interrupted progressive activity rhich has prevailed for a considerable time past. The returns sent in by the Amalgamated Society of Engineers shwa- a small increase in the number of members in receipt of out-of-work donations, not only in this district but throughout the country generally, the members now representing about two per cent. of the total membership, but the reports as to the condition of trade continue generally satisfactory. The branch returns of the Steam Engine Makers' arciety also show an increase in the number of men receiving oat-of-work support, the pro- portion of unemployed donation members being now about one per cent, but no material falling off in trade is repbrted. The retarns from all the chief Lancashire districts, except- ing Bury and St. Helens, are still of a satisfactory character. The Ironfounders' Society returns a slight decrease in the number of unemployed members, but the proportion of out- of-work .members is still large, there being out of a total membership of 11,475, not fewer than 477 on donation, besides 322 on sick relief and 372 on superannuation. The general reports as to the condition of trade can only be said to be moderate. The shipbuilding centres of the north of England continue actively employed, and in one or two dis- tricts wages are advancing. John Harley, Mayor of Rochdale, died on Wednesday - mrliin from heart disease. 12' -41 between the Yorkshire and Sussex clunty The matt. cricket teams tmilted on Wednesday in a victory for the : latter by three The Duke of Cambr.'dg.e was examined before the Channel Tunnel Committee on It.'BB4lllY' and expressed the strong .the question of Discs- : aversion with which he regend the scheme. We hear that all idea of raish;: tablishment in Scotland thissession b.ts now been given up. —Standard. On Wednesday, at a Synod of Argyll and the Isles, held in the cathedral, Cumbrae, the Very Rev. Alexacder Chin- nery Haldane was unanimously elected Bishop of Argyll and the Isles in room of the late Bishop Mackarnesti. The Prince of Wales, accompanied by his sons and the Princess Saxe-Meiningen, arrived at Portsmouth on Wednes- day, and prcceeded in the royal yacht Osborne to H.M.'s corvette Canada, lying at Spithead, in which Prince George sails as midshipman. Cheers were heartily given as the Osborne left. The Prince of Wales will steam in the Osborne as far as the Needles with the Canada, on which Prince George will then embark, the latter sailing westward. ATTICSIPTED MURDER OF Two WOMEN AT RIPLEY.—A shocking affair eccurred at Ripley on Tuesday afternoon. It appears that a man named Spick, residing at Nottingham, had been separated since February from his wife, who had gone to live with her parents at Ripley. He went there on Tuesday, and on her refusal to return to him, he shot her and her mother with a revolver, Both women were wounded in the head, and fatal results are feared. Spick was apprehended. Dr. Jerissen, the Transvaal State Advocate, - arrived in London on Wednesday morning from the continent. He had a severe attack of fever while there, but has non re- covered. He called at the Colonial Office on Wednesday to learn the decision of the Government as to a special de- legate being received from the Boer Triumvirate to negotiate upon the Transvaal Convention. Nothing has been settled yet. but Dr. Jorissen views with favour various statements that have been made by the ministers as, in his belief, indi- cating a complete and extensive inquiry into the whole question. A CONFICT BETWEEN SOLDIERS—On Monday night foor men of the Black Watch escaped from the barracks at Trip- nor Powder Magazine. Portsmouth, and were pursued by an armed picket ever hedges and wheatfields. Being ultimately overtaken they made a desperate resistance, in the course of which one of the runaways was seriously wounded in the breast by a bayonet drawn by the picket in self-defence. The injured man was conveyed to the infirmary, and another prisoner to the guard-room, but the other two Highlanders escaped, and have not yet been arrested. They lost the greater part of their clothing during the fight. The President of the Council was waited upon on Wednes- day by a deputation from the Foreign Cattle Trade Associa- tion, introduced by Mr. A. Arnold, M.P., who urged the relaxation of the stringent regulations affecting the impor- tation of foreign cattle, in the interests of the consumer. Lord Carlingford, in reply, said he viewed the deputation as a protest against any increase in stringency of regulations, or any movement in the direction of prohibition, as was desired by another representative body not long ago. The Government were acting up to the existing law, and were not disposed to strain it in any way towards further prohi- bition. _

An event which has happened at Sheffield shows that if the Deceased's Wife's Sister Bill should be passed in a form which would legalise past marriages, the result in some cases might be awkward. Some years ago a gentleman named George Smith married his deceased wife's sister, but he has since separated from her, and refused to support her. As soon as the second reading of the bill by the Lords was re- ported the lady went to Mr. Smith's house, and, having gained an entrance by breaking the windows, refused to leave, her belief being that the bill had passed. Her action was, of course, premature, and instead of regaining a home she has been fined six shillings. THE DIVISION ON THE DECEASED WIFE'S SISTER BILL. —lnconnectien with Monday night's division in the House of Lords on the bill to legalise marriage with a deceased wife's sister, it appears that the vote is the heaviest which has taken place on the subject in the Upper House. In the session of 1880 their Lordships rejected the measure by 101 to 90. Last year the adverse majority was reduced to four, the numbers being 128 for and 132 against. On each occasion had the votes of the bishops been excluded from the reckoning the bill would have been carried. Amongst the majority on Monday were the Prince of Wales and two of his brothers. LORD ALCESTER AND THE BOMBARDMENT OF ALEXAN- DRIA..—Lord Alcester, replying to the inquiries of a corres- pondent, contradicts in the clearest terms the statement of Lord Randolph Churchill in the House of Commons, last Friday, as to the action of the British Navy at Alexandria. His lordship says :—" I never bombarded the city of Alex- andria. I attacked the forts and batteries of Alexandria, situated at some distance from the city; not in consequence of the massacres, but because the party of Arabi, then in power, continued, in defiance ,of my repeated warnings, to make preparations for sinking Her Majesty's ships under my command. If I had not done so, I should have been un- worthy to hold Her Majesty's commission." THE AMALGAMATION OF MANCHESTER AND SALFORD.— The debate upon the proposed amalgamation of the borough of Salford with the city of .Manchester was resumed at an adjourned meeting of the Salford Town Council which was held on Wednesday. At the previous meeting held a week ago, a resolution was moved affirming that it is not desir- able to continue the negotiations with a view to amalgama- tion, and to this an amendment was moved referring it back to the General Purposes Committee, and instructing them to call public meetings in each of the three districts in order to obtain an expression of public opinion on the question. After a long debate the amendment was defeated, 20 voting for and 27 against it, and the original motion was carried. PRESENTATION TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF YORIC.—At the Albert Hall, Sheffield, on Tuesday, the Archbishop of York was presented with a splendid cabinet of cutlery, accom- panied by an illuminated address, expressive of the attach- ment and admiration felt for his Grace. The presentation ' entirely originated with working men of Sheffield. In his reply the Archbishop expressed his opinion that with what 1 had been already conceded, and with the changes impending, the power of the country would shortly be reposed in the working classes, who would make the laws. It was therefore of the utmost importance that the country should be go- verned, not by a thoughtless, careless people, but by those who were seriously minded to their duty to their families, their country, and their God. AN INCIDENT IN A LIVERPOOL BANK.—A. poorly-dressed young woman presented a cheque for £lOO,OOO at a Liver- pool bank a few days ago. and supported her demand for payment by saying that she had already been refused the money at three other banks. An attempt was male to in- duce her to go away, but she said she had been "humbugged enough," and would stay until she "got her rights." A policeman was then sent for, but before that invaluable representative of the law arrived the woman grabbed at a sum of over £2OO that was being passed over the counter, and secured a handful of gold. By this time the officer had arrived, and the woman was taken to the detective office, where she gave the name of " Victoria." It was intended to bring the prisoner before the magistrates, but she was found to be so hopelessly insane that she was sent to the workhouse. ENGLISH PATENTS. The following patents, amongst others published in the Commissioners of Patents Journal were sealed during the week ending June 9th, 1883 : 1 William Ford Smith and Arthur Coventry, both of Salford,' engineers, for improvements in or applicable to planing or I milling machimes. William Hargreaves and William Inglis, _Bolton, improvements in and connected with the i valves of motive power engines. Edmund Tweedale,l Accrington, improvements in machinery for spinning fibres. John Once Stetter, Snapetborpe, Wakefield, improvements in electric lamps and fittings therefor. John Henry White- head, Leeds, improvements in machinery for combing wool, cotton, silk, and other fibrous substances. James Irving, Barnsley, improvements in the shedding apparatus of looms. Thomas Brooks and Thomas Tweedale, Rtwteustall, im- provements in shuttles. John Beeby Edmondson and James Carson, Manchester, an improved method of and apparatus for dating and stamping railway tickets.—List supplied by Mr. George Davies, C.E. Feb. Inst. P.A., Patent Solicitor, 4, St. Ann's-square, Manchester. EXPECTED WINDFALL FOR A BOLTON LABOURER.— There is good reason to believe that a Mr. Costello, who recently died at Auckland, New Zealand, and left £lOO 000 to the local charities of the island, was related to a poor family resident in Bolton. Some fifty years ago a farmer of county Kildare, Ireland, broke up his home. He had three sons; one went to America. the second came to England, and the third emigrated to Australia. Up to twenty years ago the third son resided in Sydney, which place he left for Auckland, where he established a bakery and became im- mensely wealthy. A few years ago a person who had been in Mr. Costello's company at Auckland returned to Bolton, and told his brother of the great fortune of his relative. It was intended to open up communication with him, bet this was delayed, and the next news was the announcement of Mr. Costello's death. Steps are now being taken to estab- lish Mr. Costello's identity as the son of the Kildare farmer, and the brother of the Kildare farmer, and the brother of the Bolton labourer, and should these succeed, it is expec- ted that the Bolton brother will profit, as the next of kin, out of some part of the deceased's estate. The Bolton Costello is upwards of 75 years of age, and has a large family. Some time ago he was working in Hyde. GAMBLING AND GAMES or SKILL.—At the Marylebone Police Court, before Mr. De Rutzen, Harry Leonard, 24, and John Osborne, were charge with gambling with rings and a board.—lnspector Wybourn said he was on duty in plain clothes in the Edgware-road, on S tturday night, where he saw the prisoners, who had a number of walking sticks fixed upright in a hoard. Anyone who liked could have six rings for a penny, and if they threw one of the rings from a certain distance on to one of the sticks the cane became his or her property. With assistance the prisoners were apprehended. Both • prisoners protested against the charge which was brought against them. It was not gambling; it was a game of skill and jud,ginent. They commenced with 150 sticks, and at the time they were arrested they had only 10 left, and they, had not made more than half a crown by the transaction. In their opinion it was not gambling.—Mr. D. Rutzen : I am of another opinion.—The prisoner Leonard: The same sort of thing is pleyed all over ' the country. The other day this very game was played where the Prince of Wales was, and there was no attempt to put 'it down. It is as mucha game of skill as billiards. If it conies within the law against gambling of course we must suffer.—Mr. De Rutzen : In my opinion it is an offence against the law, and you are each sentenced to seven days' imprisonment with hard labour.— The prisoner Osborne said he should appeal against the decision.

TEE CORRITPT PRACTICES BILL.-The main business of the evening was the consideration of the Corrupt Practices Bill in committee, and with this measure fair progress was made. A lively debate took place on a clause proposed by Sir Trevor Lawrence making it a corrupt practice for a can- didate personalty or by deputy to subscribe before, during, or after an election, directly or indirectly, to any Society, club, or other association with a corrupt intention. Amongst others Mr. Samuel Smith strenuously opposed this proposal, on the ground that it would render legitimate charity im- possible, and ultimately the clause was withdrawn.

Evidence WAS .ben given proving that Dr. Gallagher and Wilson were staying in London from March 27th till April 4th, and were in comhZunication with the other prisoners; and Sergeant Price, of Birmingham, In- spector Black, and other officers, described the discovery of explosives in Whitehead's shop, and the circumstances under which the several prisoners were arrested. The trial was resumed on Wednesday. A considerable number of witnesses were called to trace the movements of the various members of the gang. The young man Ansburg, who had no conned, cross-examiced the police witnesses, to prove that they had offered him money and a pardon if he would give evidence, but they totally denied the imputa- tion. Evidence was given by scientific witnesses with re- gard to the highly dangerous nature of the explosives found in the possession of Whitehead, Wilson, and others, and the case for the prosecution then closed. In replying to one of the counsel for the prisoners, who denied that the charge of "levying war " against the Queen had been made out, the Lord Chief Justice said he should hold that it had, if it were shown that the prisoners had conspired among themselves to blow up buildings which were the property of the Crown.

The trial of the six "dynamite conspirators" who were charged with treason-felony was concluded on Thursday evening at the Central Criminal Court. After deliberating for an hour and 20 minutes, the jury found a verdict of guilty against Thomas Gallagher, Whitehead, Curtin, and Wilson, and acquitted Bernard Gallagher and Ansburg. The Lord Chief Justice pointed out that the prisoners, being citizens of a foreign nation, had no complaint to male against the English Government, and yet they deliberately proposed to scatter devastation and destruction broadcast. Foreigners must be shown that they could not be permitted to destroy public buildings in this country without render- ing themselves liable to heavy penalties. The four men convicted were then sentenced to penal servitude for life, the others being released. His Lordship highly commended the action of the police in the case.

It might be, he said, that they would have to take a compethi•on on these demands, but in that event, as under his new Bankruptcy Bill, they would not discharge the debtor. The audience under circumstances of great discennfort—the tall becoming insufferably hot--- listened with great attention to all the President of the Board of Trade- had to say. Mr. BRIGHT, in afterwards pro- posing a vote of thanks to the chairman, made a touching-- allusion to the eose of his lifes work, and the need therse must soon be of electing a anccessor. The, about teat o'clock, the enormous congregation slowly flowed out into. the streets, and the great demonstration was over. In continuation of the celebrations at Birmingham, a banquet to Mr. Bright was given on Thursday night in th. Town Hall. Lord Granville, in proposing the toast of "Our guests," referred to his acquaintance with Mr. Bright and Mr. Cobden in connection with the anti-corn-law agita- tion, and also his association with Mr. Bright as a colleague. in several Liberal Administrations. If any statesman of our time, he said, deserved the sympathy and admiration, of his fellow countrymen it was Mr. Bright. He asked them to bear in mind some of the great questions that had been settled during the. last 40 years, and which leaders of the Liberal party like Mr. Br,ght had earnestly advocated ; for example, Bee repeal of the corn laws, the repeal of the navigation laws, and the liberation of our tariff from protectionist duties. In conclusion, Earl Granv ills paid a high tribute to Mr. Bright's political honesty and inteeTity.—Mr. Bright, in responding, spoke of the various questions in which he had taken part, iscluding his opposition to the distraint for Church rates at Rochdale, electoral reform, the government of India, the Crimean war, and Ireland. Speaking of the House of Commons, be said there were at present sums members on the Conservative side who had abindoned the character and conduct of gentlemen, and had repudiated the of the majority of the constituencies. Those members were determined if possible that the majority of the constituences should fail in their efforts and at this moment were in alliance with an Irish rebel party, the ' main portion of whose funds, for the purposes of agitatation, came directly from avowed enemies of England, and whose oath of allegiance was broken by asscciation with these enemies of the country. The great constituenciet must look to this, and preserve the honour and free-work- ing of the House of Commons. The reform that was c, ming must crush the power and close the career of the mem who now afflicted the House, and who, from night to night, insulted the majesty of the British people. Mr John Stagg, M.P., was also amongst the speakers. A torchlight pro- cession escorted Lord Granville and Mr. Bright through the town.

div.head: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
div.p: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.

HOUSE OF LORDS.—MOIDAY. MARRIAGE WITH A DECEASED WIFE'S SISTER. --- The second reading of the Deceased Wife's Sister Bill was moved by the Earl of DALHOUSIE, sho complained of the action of the prelates in opposition to it as misleading, in- asmuch as it was supposed from the coarse Shay took that the bill was hostile to the principles of religion and morality, which was not the case. His Lordship pointed out that marriages with a deceased wife's sister were legal in nearly all the colonies, and that the bill had been passed seven times by the Commons—Earl CAIRNS moved the rejection of the bill, and asked where was the security, if this hill were passed, that they would not be asked to go much further. He contended that the bill proposed to establish a sort of morganatic marriage which could only be valid before the registrar. The bill provided that these marriages should not take place in churches, as he thought for the obvious reason that they would offend religious feeling He was unable to see that there was any difference between a marriage with a deceased wife's sister and a marriage with a deceased husband's brother.—Lord BRAMWELL supported the bill, regarding the existing law as 4 cruel and mis- chievous one, for which he could see no justification.—The Archbishop of CANTERBURY defended the action of the Episcopal bench, and argued that the abrogation of the ex- isting law would bring misery and wretchedness into thou- sands of families.—The second reading of the bill was car- ried by 185 votes against 158, a majority of seven in favoar of the measure. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MONDAY.

BRinsa MWACHANTS sic TIIRKEY.—Lord E. FurztaAu- incE,stated that as the British merchants in Turkey had not protested against the imposition of the 8 per cent ad valorem duties, our Charge d' illaires at Constantinopl, had been instructed to accept them with a reserve on the part of our Government as to the action of the Porte in suddenly bringing the new tariff into force in disregard of the assurance given that no change would be made before October next. _ _

—„--. MADAGASCAR.—In answer to Mr. Arnold, Lord EDMOND FITZMAIIRICE said that no representations other than thuse contained in the blue books presented to Parliament bad been made to the French Government with regard to Madagascar.

THE SERIOUS CHARGE AGAINST THE KHEDIVE.—Lord R. CHURCHILL wished to knw whether the Government had since Friday inquired into the charge against the Khedive of having been concerned in the instigation of the massacre at Alexandria.—Mr. GLADSTONE read despatches from Sir E. Malet, Major Macdonald, and Lord Dufferin. The one from Lord Dufferin to Lord Granville was to the effect that the accusation against the Khedive could not be supported by any tangible fact or circumstance which could bring conviction to reasonable minds, and that during the whole of his stay in Egypt not a tittle of evidence was brought to his notice which would in the faintest degree have authorised so strange an allegation. His Lordship added that he had never been able to come to any ' other conclusion than that the calumny in question was one of those thoasand baseless fabrications which teem from the Egyptian soil —Sir S. NORTHCOTE asked if the Government would give the House the several telegrams which had passed between our Government and our representatives in Egypt, or with the Egyptian Government. on the subject of Suleiman's execution.—Lord E. FITZMAURICE replied that it would be better that the House should have the full infor- mation rather than that he should produce it piecemeal. The information was part of the promised papers, which would be presented at once.—Sir S. NORTHCOTE moved the adjournment of the House for the purpose of calling attention to a matter of urgent public importance. He thought the House ought to know the nature of the telegram sent by Lord Granville to Sir E. Malet, and the exact time at which it was sent.—Lord E. FITZMATIRICE said the Government never had any doubt after the infor- mation which reached them that Suleiman Sarni was to be executed that the sentence was a fair and just one. In con- sequence of disturbing statements in the papers, the Go- vernment decided to put themselves in possession of Major Macdonald's opinion. After the discussion on Friday two telegrams were sent, and they received in reply the opinion of Major Macdonald that Suleiman Sarni deserved his fate. —Lord R. CHURCH/LL argued that the Government did not wish to save Suleiman Sami's life, and were perfectly aware that it would be more convenient to the puthorities in Egypt that he should be hanged. He asserted that the order to open fire on the English fleet, which produced the bombard- ment of Alexandria and led to the destruction of the town was signed by the Khedive, and that Her Majesty's Govern- ment was as directly connected with the hanging of Sulei- man Semi as of Timothy Kelly. Therefore he was justified in charging the Government with having been responsible for the grossest and foulest judicial murder that ever stained the annals of Oriental justice, and he challenged the Prime Minister to divest himself or his colleagues of responsibility for the assassination of Suleiman Sami.—Mr. GLADSTONE, in replying to the violent criticisms of Lord Randolph, remarked that if the noble Lord were under some sense of responsibility he would not throw out these scandalous and shameful charges against the ruler of Egypt and the judges' including the English members of the Court. He was hound to say that everything he had beard gave him reason to believe that not only was Suleiman Sami guilty of the crime for which he was executed, but that the circumstances of his guilt as indicated by his conduct on the day of the burning of Alexandria were circumstances of great aggravation. He reminded the House that in 1882 the Government had given a pledge not to take any steps to prevent execution in cases such as taking part in the burning of Alexandria.—After further discussion the motion for the adjournment was negatived without a division, and the House went into committee on Lord Alcester's Annuity Bill.

THE Arrigurri Brra..—The debate on the motion to go into committee on the Lord Alcester Annuity Bill was then resumed, and after some words from Mr. Biggar and Mr. Waddy the House divided, agreeing to go into committee by 229 votes against 45. Opposition was renewed in committee, but eventually the Bill passed without amendment. The Lord Wolseley's Grant Bill afterwards passed through com- mittee.

div.head: HOUSE OP LORDS.-TUESDAY.
div.p: HOUSE OP LORDS.-TUESDAY.

The Municipal Corporations (Unreformed) Bill and the Cathedral Statutes Bill passed through committee, and several measures were advanced a stage. There was a short debate on the state of the army, particularly in reference to recruiting, and a conversation on the condition of the naval station since the practical reueal of the Contagious Diseases Act.

div.head: HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TtrEsDAY.
div.p: HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TtrEsDAY.

A new writ was issued for the county of Monaghan in the room of Mr. John Givan.—Lord E. FITZNIALTRICE informed Sir H. Wolff that he did not intend to lay on the table a copy of the letter originally written by Lord Granville to Mr. Errington.—The CHIEF SECRETARY for IRELAND stated that in consequence of the boast of one of the Invincibles that he had poisoned Mr. Jury, the Dub'in hotelkeeper, the body had been exhumed, and no trace of poison was dis- covered.—Colonel DAWNAY explained that a question pur by him last week which contained an imputation upon the Gaekwar of Baroda related to another native prince, and that Lord Ripon took no action of any kind in reference to the affair.—The House went into Committee on the Corrupt Practices Bill.—At the evening sitting Lord GEORGE HAMILTON moved that an immediate revision of the pur- chase clauses of the Irish Land Act, 1881, was necessary in order to give effect to the intentions of Parliament, and to make the clauses a reality.—The motion was seconded by Mr. A. BALFOIJR.-1111% TEEVELYAN stated that the Govern- ment would assent to the proposal for a revision of the clauses if they were not asked to undertake immediate legislation in that direction.

div.head: HOUSE OF COMMONS.--WEDNEsDAy.
div.p: HOUSE OF COMMONS.--WEDNEsDAy.

POOR-LAW GUARDIANS (IRELAND) BILL.—Mr. M•CoAN moved the second reading of the Poor-law Guardians (Ire- land) Bill. The bill proposed to substantially change the present system of election by substituting ballot for open ! voting, and triennial for annual election. The bill also pro- vided that votes should be given in person.—Col. KING. HARMAN moved the rek.etion of the bill.—After fui tiler discussion, Mr. TREVELYAN thought the debate showed the strength of opinion in favour of the bill, which essentially carried out the application of the system of ballot to poor- law elections. 'The Government had promised, if they found time, to bring in a bill dealing with the question. The bill was read a second time. THE EMPLOYERS' LIABILITY ACT.—Mr. BURT moved the second reading of the Employers' Liability Act (1880) Amendment Bill. He stated that after the Employers' Liability Act was passed, pressure was brqught to bear upon the workmen, in many cases compelling them to contract themselves out of the provisions of the bill. In Lancashire more than 27,000 miners, by unfair pressure, were compelled to sign papers foregoing any claims under the Act. The ob- ject of the bill was to prevent those contracts being signed under pressure by making them illegal.—Sir JOSEPH PEASE moved an amendment to the effect " That it is enexpedient to interfere with the freedom of contract between employers and employed which enables them to contract themselves out of the Act of 1880." On a division the amendment was carried by 140, against 38 votes. • HOUSE OF LORDS.—TUURSDAY.

Lord DERBY made gn important statement with regard to the affairs of Basutoland. He reviewed the circumstances under which recent difficulties had arisen, and said it had been determined to restore the connection which had for- merly existed between the Bisutos and the Imperial Govern- ment, if the natives were willing to accept such a solution. The country would not be treated as a Crown colony, but would be granted Home Rule' in the strictest sense of the word
