div.head: STATE OF IRELAND.
div.p: THE STATE OF IRELAND.

Mr. J. F. Small, a Parnellite, was elected on Wednesday as a representative of county Wexford without opposition. A decision of the Irish Common Pleas on Monday leaves James Carey still a m.mber of the Dublin Town Council, despite the resolution vacating his seat and the subsequent election of another person. Owing to the Piatidtial Anthem being first on the musical programme at the demonstration on the opening of the Cork Exhibition, a number of bands have refused to take part in it.
A fight took place in G away on Wednesday night be- tween Militia and the Suff )Ik regiment. Belts were freely used, and many serious wounds were inflicted before order was restored.

At Cashel, on Thursday morning, when Dr. Leech, the Dean of Cashel, was driving to the railway station, the horse became frightened at the music of a passing band. The dean was thrown off the car and sustained severe injuries, his ankle bone being broken and his wrist sprained. At the Dublin Police Court on Tuesday, three ejectment summonses, issued in the came of the son of the informer Jarhes Carey. were entered on the list. The defendants are Carey's tenants, who, since he became informer, had stated their determinati3n not to pay rent to him. None of the parties, however, appeared, and the cases fell through. THE LATE Mn.. Judy.—The examination of the stomach and intestines of the late Mr. Jury, rendered necessary by the publication of the s:ory that he had been poisoned, has been completed, with the result that no trace of any poison of any kind has been found, nor were there any indications leading to the supposition that Mr. Jury died from any other cause than that assigned by his medical attendants.

div.head: BRIGHT CELEBRATION.
div.p: THE BRIGHT CELEBRATION.

The Right Hon. John Bright arrived at Stratford-on- Avon on Saturday evening from London, and was met at the railway station by Mr. R. Curry, his son-in-law, with whom be stayed until Monday. Mr. Bright was looking remarkably well. Throughout Saturday the Birmingham Town Hall was thronged with persons, the illuminated ad- dress of the Birmingham Liberal Association and the dessert service, to be presented to Mr. Bright, being on view. The service consists of a centrepiece and plateau, two end pieces, and four compotiers, en suite' in the renaissance style, and is of oxydised silver, relieved with dead gilding. On the centrepiece is the following inscription :—" Presented to the Right Hon. John Bright, M.P., by the Birmingham Liberal Association, on the completion of his twenty-fifth year as member for the borough. June, 1883." On Satur- day, the statue of the late Mr. J. S. Wright, M.P., which is to be unveiled by Mr. Bright, was placed upon the pedestal in front of the Council House, amidst the ringing cheers of a crowd numbering several thousand persons. The statue was covered with drapery, and will not be seen until the unveiling ceremony. On Monday a large crowd assembled at Stratford-nn-Avon Railway Station shortly before 12 o'clock to witness the de- parture of Mr. Bright for Birmingham. The right hon. gentleman was accompanied by his eldest son and daughter and several personal friends. . The party travelled in a saloon carriage by special train to Birmingham, where the Mayor, Corporation, and members of the Liberal Association awaited Mr. Bright. As the train steamed out of the statien Mr. Bright was loudly cheered by the crowd. Punctually at 12-30 the train arrived at Small fleatheStatione The right hon. gentleman and his party were at once conducted to a waiting room, where they were received by Mr. Dixon and the Mayor. After a quarter of an hour's delay, caused by the tardy appearance of the Reception Committee, owing to the crowded state of the station, the whole party came out on to the platform, and bouquets having been presented to the ladies, a photograph of a group, composed as follows, was taken :—Mr. John Bright, Mr. and Mrs. Albert Bright, , Mr. and Mrs. Curry, Mrs. Bernard Roth, the Mayor (Mr. 1 Alderman White), Mr. Schnadhorst, Mr. Powell Williamsil anti Dr. Dale. Among others on the platform were Mr. Wig- gin, M.P., Mr. Jesse Collings, M.P., aad Sir John Bennett. ' Mr. George Dixon, president of the Liberal Association and member for the borough from 1867 to 1876, then I stepped forward and asked Mr. Bright's acceptance of a gold medal bearing upon it the old election cry of "Peace, Retrenchment, and Reform," and recording the fact that Mr. Bright was elected M.P. for Birmingham in 1857. In reply, the veteran statesman said he looked forward to the events of the present week with no little apprehension, but he was sure that everything that could be done to miti- gate his miefortune was done by the kindness of his friends. He declared that there were few, if any, members who ba& been treated with the consideration, generosity, sympathy, and assistance which he had received during his representa- tion of Birmingham. He owed his constituents a debt of gratitude he could never repay. Commemorative medals were then handed to the ladies by Masters Schnadhorst and Williams, after which the party proceeded to a house close by until the procession was ar- ranged, after which Mr. Bright joined it. He was received with tremendous cheering when the assembled thousands caught sight of him. A procession, headed by the Fire Brigade, and consisting of members of the Birmingham and South Staffordshire Trade Councils and of several temper- ance societies, delegates from Liberal associations in various parts of the country, members of all the ward branches of the Birmingham Liberal Association, and the local Liberal clubs, were marshalled to receive the right hon. gentleman, and after the singing of a song of welcome to the tune of "Johnny comes marching borne again," started for the Aeton Lower Ground. Several thousand persons took part in the procession' which was nearly two miles long. Mr. bright rode in the Mayor's carriage at the rear of the proces- sion, and was enthusiastically received. The whole of the route from the station to the park, five miles distance, was lined with people, who gave the right hon. gentleman a truly royal reception. lie left the precession at one point, and proceeded to the offices of the Aston Local Board, from whence he watched it pass by. It is computed that upwards of 200,000 persons were in the streets along which the pro- cession passed. Mr. Bright had a day of rest on Tuesday. He stayed at The Dales, Edebaston, the house of Mr. George Dixon. The celebration was continued on Wednesday by the presentation of addresses, dtc., to the right hon. gentleman at an immense gathering in Bingley Hall. The chair was taken by Mr. G. Dixon, president of the Liberal Association, and Mr. Chamberlain, M.P., was among those present. Altogether about 160 addresses were presented.—Mr. Bremer; on rising to address the meeting, was received with loud and cqntinuous cheering. The right hon. gentleman seemed much affected. His voice was a little thick when he began, but it resumed its silver tone before he had got through the sentence in which, in graceful fashion, he expressed his ob- ligations. He got into the subject by taking up some un- friendly criticisms, in which it was complained that in his speeches he always went back into past times and raked up old facts. He thought himself this was a wise thing to do, and if it had been more generally done needless and san- guinary wars in which the country had embroiled itself might have been avoided. His unfriendly critics, he was afraid, found nothing in the past which supported them in their policy, and that was no doubt the reason of their aversion to comparisons with old times. THE MURDER OF Loa. MOHNTMORRES.—A man named Patrick Sweeney, who a few days sinc-3 abruptly left Cong, county Mayo, where police inquiries were being instituted, was on Tuesday arrested at Queenstown, charged with being the murderer of Lord Mountinorres, who was shot in Mayo ahout two years ago. Sweeney had intended sailing for New York on Wednesday. In a letter to United Ireland the mother of Timothy Kelly, who was executed for the Phosoix Park murders, says :—My son Tim has died, but lam consoled by the knowle4e that he died as hundreds of true Irishmen died before, firm in his faith and in his patriotism. In my great grief I have found many friends, and to all those whose sympathy has been given to me I return my most sincere thanks.

Mr. Givan, who la%s been appointed Crown Solicitor for the counties of Meath and Kildare, has resigned his seat for county Monaghan. An interesting contest is promised for. the seat. Three candidates are likely to take part in it— Mr. Monroe, Q,C., on behalf of the Conservatives, Mr. Chas. M'Ardle as representing the Home Rulers, and Mr. T. M. Healy on behalf of the advanced Irish piny. Mr. Healy proposeS to resign his seat for Wexford is order to take part in the contest. _ _

_ THE RESIGNATION OF LOUD SPENCER.—It is DOW prac- tically settled that Lord Spencer, on his own strongly-urged : request, is to be released from the position of Irish Viceroy. No choice, or indication of a choice, of his successor has yet been made, and the names hitherto mentioned are mere guesses. The new Viceroy will not be in the Cabinet, it being desired to give Mr. Trevelyan a full opportunity of displaying his individuality in the new chapter of Irish administration, which, it is alleged, will be directed to allaying the irritation caused- by recent events. , THE PRCENIX PARE MURDERS: GOYERNMENTREWARDS. —The following are the rewards which have been made in connection with the Plecenix Park murders and the success- ful investigation of the case t—lrtobart Farrell, £1,000; Alice Carroll, £500; Kavanagh. £5OO and pardon; Lamie, £250 ; Smith, £250; Noad, £10; Huxley, £250; Emma Jones, £100; Mottley, £250 and passage paid; Hands and Wife, £3OO ; Joe Hanlon, £5O; Treynor, £2O; McKeown and Mclneney, each £6O and petteege paid; Godden, £250; Superintendent Mallon, £l,OOO ; and four members of his staff, £lOO each. EXECUTION OF KELLY.—Timothy Kelly, one of the Phcenix Park assassins, was hanged on Saturday. He made no statement. Kelly was the youngest of the band of mur- derers, and his conviction was only obtained on the third trial. There was the usual assemblage outside the gaol at the time of the execution, but no demonstration calling for the pace of the authorities. In all six men were condemned to death for complicity in the crime of the Oth May, 1882; one was reprieved, and the execution of Kelly completes the hangmen's part in the terrible drama—at all events, for the present. There is reason to believe that the authorities in Dublin have been informed of the existence of a secret society re- cently formed, the object of which is the removal of all in- formers, and the informer James Carey in particular, and that they, with this in view, refuse at present to allow him to go outside Kilmainham gaol. The houses in which the members of this society are supposed to meet are being closely watched by detectives, aud a raid recently made on one of these houses proving fruitless, the police charged the proprietor with selling liqnor during unlicensed hours. It is further added that the police have declined to be respon- sible for James Carey should he be set at large. FOURTEEN THOUSAND PERSONS IN A STATE OF PAUPER- Ism.—Mr. Ernest Hart, who, accompanied by an agricul- tural expert, has jest made a tour of investigation in various parts of Ireland under the auspices of the Irish Political Committee, found that 14,000 persons in Donegal are being supported by alms, and that the emigration of the active and able-bodied poor is increasing, the proportion of those who remain being dependent on charity. Mr. Hart adds that there are in Ireland 4,000,000 acres of neglected grass land, with regard to which he will recumrnend in hie report that the Government be urged to advance to a responsible corn- piny such sums as will reclaim the land so going to waste, and enable tenants to be placed on to s of about 30 acres, with a view to their ultimately becoming peasant proprietors. Joe Poole was charged in a Dublin Police Court. on Wednesday, with the murder of John Kenny, in July last. Kenny was a Step ienite Fenian, and as he WAS believed to have given information it was resolved to kill him. Poole was a centre "of the society and on very intimate terms with Kenny, and on the night of the murder he went to Kenny's house and spent the evehinc drinking whisky in his company. Ahem. midnight Kenny went out with Poole to see him to the end of the lane and never returned, his body, severely stabbed, being foutel under a neighbouring railway bridge. Poole, Curley, and a man named Doyle were arreseed for the crime, but were dischaNted, and it was riot until William Larnie, in the recent investigation into the proceedings of the Dublin Fenians. incriminated Poole that a definiec eine could be obtained to the perpetrators of the assa s,i nation.

div.head: 14'oREIGN INTELLIGENCE.
div.p: 14'oREIGN INTELLIGENCE.
THE EXPLOSION AT SCUTARI : 150 PERSONS KILLED.

It is now stated from Vienna that the effect of the explo- sion caused by lightning in the Scutari powder magazine. reported a couple of days ago, was more serious than was at fist reported, 150 persons, soldiers and civiliane, being killed. and 53 wounded. Two hundred barrels of gunpowder And 6000 cartridges exploded, 40 workshops being totally destroyed. The lightning has also been doing great damage in other quarters. A few days ago three workmen were, killed near Laibach, and on Tuesday afternoon a girl was killed in the Vienna streets.

The Treaty of Commerce between Great Britain and Italy will probably be signed on Thursday next. A disastrous accident is reported from Kaloge. Tim* stories of the Tula Barracks in that town suddenly fell. Tea people were killed and a large number injured. It is reported from Teheran that Russia is seeking e. " rectification " of her frontier by an exchange of territory with Panda.
The Chief Commissioner in British Barmah has com- muted the death sentence passed on the Shan Prince t• transportation for life. _ _

Vienna newspaper states that famine prevails in many districts of Asia Minor, that many deaths have already oe• curred, and that grain has increased sixfold in value. Hicks Pasha has sent a message from the Soudan to asy that he requires 3,000 more men to re•establish order at Kor- dofan. General Wood, who has been applied to, refuses to despatch any more of his men. The official organ of the Montenegrin Government save that the insurrection against the Turkish power in Albania has been suppressed. On the other hand, despatches re- ceived from Constantinople at Vienna and Varna state that severe fighting continues. Seventeen lives were lost and 55 persons were injured by the explosion of the powder magazine in the fortress of Scu- tari on Friday last. There was a great destruction of pro- perty, caused by one side of the fortress falling upon the bazaar.

General Crook is reported to have returned from his Mexican expedition against the Apache Indians. Two hun- dred and thirty of the Indians surrendered to him. He lost none of his men, but the 'Rain Apache force seems to have eluded him, returning to Arizona in detached bands. The Indians have started extensive prairie fires in Mexico.

A Times telegram from Durban says that "all sorts of rumours" are current with regard to the state of affairs in Zululand. It is reported that Nunn, the English "adviser" of Okam, has bean murdered, after the defeat of that chiere people by a tribe who are friendly to Cetewayo. The Standard's correspondent states that the general condition of Zululand is one of anarchy and bloodshed. The Russian Coronation festivities have been appropriately concluded by the triumphal entry of the Czar and Czarina into St. Petersburg on Sunday. Dense crowds thronged the streets, and their Majesties met with a grand and appatently loyal reception. The line of route was artistically decorated. and there was no lack of enthusiastic cheering. The city was brilliantly illuminated in the evening. ExEcnnoN OF SULEIMAN SAML—Suleiman Sami, who was found guilty on Thursday of complicity in massacre and plunder and sentenced to death by court-martial, was hanged on Saturday morning at Alexandria in the middle of the ruins of the Great Square. It is stated that the exe- cution took place on the spot where Suleiman Sarni had been seen smoking and directing the incendiaries. BRITISH BURMAIL—A PRLNCE SENTENCED TO DEATH The judges of the Special Court have delivered judgment in the appeal of the Shan Prince, who was lately convicted of I murder and sentenced to death by the Recorder of Rangoon. I The accused pleaded that he was a sovereign prince, and not, subject to the jurisdiction. The Court held that although Shan Isabwah may possess powers which ordinarily belong only to sovereign princes, still the recognition of his position as such by other States is wholly wanting. The appeal, therefore, is dismiesed, and the sentence of death is , confirmed. . . _

THREE PERSONS MURDERED.—Advices from PernambnCO report the mur.lqr of three inembas of a distinguished family. Manoel Antonio da Silveira Lessa, aged E 44 married to his cousin, 18 years of age, was attacked by hio cousin, Clodoaldo de Azevede Lessa, and mortally wounded by a revolver shot. While the wounded man WAS la (no agonies of death, his hro•her Pedro stole upstairs to wnere his sister-in-law and her mother were weeping, and, rnehing on his sister-in-law, stabbed her six times with a knife. The mother sought to save her daughter, but was strut* down with three wounds. Pedro, who wls secured by (tie police, declares that he was actuatedlbv a desire to avenge his brother's death upon her, who, he believed, had either caused it or contributed to it. The young woman, however, is said to have declared before she died that she was en- tirely innocent of any part in the murder of her husband. TEnurnr.E. EXPLOSIONS IN AMERICA: SEVERAL MEG( BLOWN TO PlECES.—lnformation has been received frail Cleveland, Ohio, of a disastrous boiler explosion in the 811.11 mills of Mr. Chandler, at Leon, Trumbull County. The village of Leon consists of some eight or nine dwellings apt a SAW mill, recently erected by the owner. Shortly after noon on the 25th ult. a terrific explosion was heard, and the whole of the mill was eompletely demolished. There were four employes in the mill at the time and a neighbouring farmer. One man was blown 100 feet into the air, and hla body was shockingly mangled when found. Another man was blown through the walls of the building, whilst the remainder were found in a shockingly mutilated condition. Not a vestige of the mill remained standing. The explosion was heard ten miles distant, and there was immense excite- ment in the surrounding district. Another boiler explosion took place in a saw mill at Waterford, Spencer County, and the owner of the mill was instantly killed, as well as several of the workmen.

• RAILWAY ACCIDENT AT NEWTON STATION.—SESIOUS INTERRUPTION OF TRAFFIC.—An accident, resulting le serious interruption of traffic, and a complete block of the "down" line for several hours, occurred at Newton Brilge Station, on Starchy morning last. The passenger train leaving Manchester at 8 45 a.m. and due at Earlestown at 10 o'clock, arrived a Newton Bridge Station about 9-65; ' and after some of the rvsengers bad alighted, was, as usual being shunted into a siding to allow the 9-25 train from Wigan to enter the station, when two of the carriages in the centre of the train, caught the facing points and were thrown off the metals. Several persons were in the carriages, hot beycnd a slight shaking, no one received any injury. The- train from Wigan to Warrington, was unable to draw up in the station, and all the passengers consequently alighted and entered the fore-part of the Manchester and Liverpool train, which • bad • fortunately remained upon the rails. The engine attached to two of the carriages of the latter train, then proceeded to Warrington, and from these the passengers by the two trains proceedt4 to their respective destinations, a special train being despatched to Liverpool. A break-down gang was teleg#aph,d for to Warrington, but owing to the day twing Sunday the men did not put in an appearance until I about one o'clock. Fortunately not very many trains were I passing as the traffic bad to be worked on a single line, and the "down" line was not clear until about four o'clock.

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, JUNE 16, 1883.

The people of Birmingham have this week. been engaged in doing honour to their senior tepresentative, and we may say that in se doing they have also done honour to thaw selves. It is not given to every constituenci to be represented by a member combining s°. many of the rare qualities of StatesmanshiP which are to be found in that Tribune of the. People, Mr. BRIGHT, and for the very reasoit that he has throughout his long political career endeared himself more than any other public man to the working classes, whom ir it has been his one desire to serve and t° elevate, it is not surprising that the connec; tion between him and his constituency shoulo, have for fully a quarter of a century remainee so cordial. Indeed, any and every constitty • ency should be proud to have a person of se much nobility of character to represent : Nor can we wonder that there should have sprang up in the breasts of the people Of Birmingham so spontaneous a desire to commemorate in a befitting manner his twenty - five years faithful service; there would have been cause for stir' prise had an event so interesting bee° allowed to slip unnoticed. This, however, was not the case, and the festivities of the week, which have been princely in the,ir magnificence, amply testify to the affection le which Mr. BRIGHT is held not only by 11)5 constituents, but by the nation at large. l‘i_Ar" BRIG/1T is now in his 73rd year, he enters public life when only zo years of age, conse- quently he has been before the country full); , half a century. There is no public movemel' during that period in which he has not take° ' an active part; and it is a pleasure to reflec", that he has lived long enough to witness nearly every refoqn with which he has.beell identified if not actually accomplished, a; least on the eve of being so His brilliant , and persuasive oratory, his unswerving devo: tion to principle, his remarkable courage, h's perseverance, and his determination of char; acter, have alike been wielded on behall more especially of th:-; poor and the 01?' pressed, and though during his lifetime 131 motives have often been misunderstood all`: as frequently misrepresented—and he ha' been made, in' fact, to suffer temporal"' martyrdom for his zeal in more than one righteous cause—he is now reaping the merited reward of his arduous and self-dellr ing labours in the public weal. The agitatio° of 1831-32 first drew forth the right hoi?. gentleman's sympathies and exercised 121 powers, and during that memorable perio_by he availed himself of every opportunity OP presented itself to lift his eloquent voice 10 favour of an extended franchise; but it via not until Mr. BRIGHT joined the movement for the abolition of the duty on corn thak he gave promise of his future greatness' We believe it is chiefly for the able assistance he rendered to COBDEN and the League ill securing the repeal of the corn laws that big name and fame will be cherished by futUre generations. He was first returned 10 Parliament as the representative of the county of Durham in 1843, and his maideo speech was delivered on the free trade question. His early utterances were re- ceived with derison on the Tory benches' but he soon began to make his influencei felt, and his opponents were compelie, not only to listen to him, but to answ7; if they could, his powerful arguments. While member for Durham he, along with Con Dir and other members of the Anti-Corn Leaglre' addressed meetings here, there, and everc where; deluged the country with the.',o literature; and educated the people 1.. the principles of their organisati% until at length they succeeded ,2e converting the Prime Minister of r„„" day, Sir R. PEEL—once their promising opponent—to their- views. 11:1,1 repeal of the corn laws soon folloWed, famine then rapidly spreading was averte; and the untold benefits to- millions of Pecti which have followed in the wake of the recou,, of these laws it is impossible to over-estitnalL As Mr. BRIGHT stated on Wednesday, _l-11 sweeping away protection the wages of ag_i'd cultural labourers had been increased their position improved, artisans' wages. been advanced 50 or 6o per cent., an wages of domestic servants had been double" There are of course, legislators like t.. 11 Duke of RUTLAND, for instance. who Wow t"; have us believe that agriculture is going "rack and ruin" and that the only cure _ul, 101 it is a return to Protection. The noble d has; happily, but few followers, and we.at.r., inclined to hail the adoption of free trade aosthmerorceoucnalteruielsa.tedantdo egsipveecrieall ileyfbtyoAaniger irc7l:

Variety classes: Any other variety classes over 301bs. weight.-1, Robert Hood Wright, Newton Hall, Newton-le-Willows. CURIOUS CASE OF MISTAKEN IDENTITY AT ST. HELENS. —A young man named Joseph Towey, living at Ashcroft- street, Parr, was on Monday charged at the St. Helens Police Court with indecent behaviour, and also with as- saulting P.C. Colquhonn. Colquhonn stated that at ten minutes past eleven on Saturday night he was on duty in Church-street and saw the defendant go past in company with an immoral woman who was well known to the police. He followed them to Travis-street, Parr, and owing to their indecent behaviour in an entry he apprehended the female. Defendant, however, attempted to rescue her, and witness was at length obliged to let her go. and apprehend defen- dant. The latter was very violent and made a continued ambit on witness, on one occasion knocking him to the grorind, and ultimately, with the assistance of a crowd, es- caped with the handcuffs on his left wrist. A search was afterwards made at Collins Green for him, but finally be was arrested at his father's house about half-past five on Sunday morning.—P.C. Carruthers, who was present at the arrest, said there were no marks on defendants wrist such as might have been caused by handcuffs.—Mr. J. 0. Swift, who de- fended, said that was a case of mistaken identity. The defendant was a young man of irreproachable character, and the officer Colquhotin, who had only been seven weeks in the force, had evidently made a complete mistake.—Witnesses named Thomas Platt, Joseph Tither, and William Twist were called and stated that a man came to them late on Saturday night with a pair of handcuffs on and asked for the loan of a chisel to strike them off. They, however, refused to have anything to do with him. This man was not the defendant. He told Twist that he be- longed to Earlestown, and went away in the direction of Parr Stocks.—The Chairman (Mr. R. Pilkineton) said there could be no doubt it was a case of mistaken identity, and therefore the defendant, who was no • doubt a respectable young man, would be discharged.—Eliz ibeth Druminciud, the woman who was alleged to have been in the c impaby of the last-named defendant, was sent to gaol for a month.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 16, 1883 ST. AMBROSE CHURCH, WIDNES. 1 RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 16, 1883 ST. AMBROSE CHURCH, WIDNES. 1 RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

COAL SHIPPED FROM RUNCORN.—From a parliamentary' paper issued on Saturday, it appears that 62,920 tons of coal was shipped at Runcorn during 1882. Sr. Joule's PRIESEYTERIAN CHAPEL, RUNCORN —ln aid of the funds of this chapel, two sermens were preached on Sunday by the Rev. Professor lelwarde eI.A. of 3ala College. The collections reelized £6 OPCN-AIR CONC Ears AT RuNCORN. The Runcorn Pariah Church band played a selection of music on the marett ground on Thureley. As usual a geat number of people assembled to hear the sweet strains. WIDNES WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL —rile anniversary sermons in aid of this school were preeceeu on undey morning and evening by the Rev. C W. L Christien, of Burslem, in Victoria-road Chapel. There were crowded congregations on each occasion. In the afternoon Mr. John Simpson, of Runcorn. delivered an address to the scholars in Lacey-street school. The collections for the day amounted to £5O is Bd. RUNCORN AND THE SHIP Cat-rale—The Ship Canal Cemmittee of the Board of Commissioners haying obtained powers to visit London at the last meeting of the Board, lost no time in doing so. On Thursday', last week, a deputation journeyed to the Metropolis, where they had an interview with the promoters of the ship canal. Consequent upon this visit, an "informal meeting" of the Board of Cotnrsis- sioners was held at half-past eight on Wednesday morning. About four members failed to put in an appearance. The object of the meeting was to consider a number of clauses which had been drafted by the law clerk (Mr. Linaker), but the reporters were refused admission, and the public must remain in ignorance of their representatives' course of action. ECCENTRIC CONDUCT AT WIDNES.— Al Widnes Petty Sessions on Wednesday, Patrick McGarten, a middle aged man, apparently a lab Curer, was charged with wandering abroad —P.C. Heaton said at half-pas e two on that morning he saw the prisoner jumping up and down and conducting himself in a very straoge manner in Waterloo-road. Mr. Lewin (deputy magistrates' clerk): Do you think he is re- sponsible for his actions? Well, I don't think he is in his right mind.—The prisoner: I am right enough; lam as right as you are.—The magistrates thought it best to have the prisoner medically examined, and remanded him until the following thy. Subsequently the prisoner was again placed in the duck and discharged, the examination having apparently shown that the prisoner had been drinking. CHANGE RINGING AT RUNCORN.—On Saturday afternoon a mixed company of ricgers occupied the tower of Runcorn Parish Church, and attempted to ring Holt's ten-part peal of grandsire triples, 5,040 changes; but after ringing 2,500, " stand " was called owing to a change place. The ringers were the following :—S. Hoxworth, Runcorn, (treble) J. Davidson, Liverpool, 2; C. Sharpies, Aughton, 3; J. Large, Farnvrorth, 4 ; J. R. Pi itchard, Liverpool, conductor, 5 ; J. Latchford, F aniworth, 6; J. Aspinall, Liverpool, 7; and T. Williamson, Runcorn, (tenor). the following ringers who are members of the Lancashire Association of Change Ringers, afterwards rang a peal of grandsires minor, 720 changes, in 26 minutes :—J. Davidson, (treble), J. Large, 2; J. Aspinall, 3; A. T. Lowe, 4; C. Sharpies, 5 ; J. Latch- ford, conductor, (tenor). ASSAULT By A SEA CAPTAIN AT RUNCORN.—At Run- corn Police Court, on Tuesday, before Mr. J.ihn Brundrit and Captain C. W. Hazlehurst, John Brown, a see captain, was brought up in custody charged with with being drunk and disorderly in Church-street, and also with having at the police station assaulted P.C. Finney. kbout 11 o'clock on the previous night, P.C. Fiuney saw the prisoner, who was drunk, insulting the passengers in Church-street, and otherwise misbehaving himself. The constable was com- pelled to take him into custody, when he became very violent, and with considerable difficulty he was conveyed to the police station. While being searched there he struck Finney a violent blow on the chest; and so uproarious was his conduct, that the aid of Supt. Williamson was required to remove him to the cells. He was fined 10s. and costs on each charge, or, in default, a month's hard labour. A STRUGGLE* 'WITH A WIDNES LUNATIC.—Mr. Scannell, the relieving officer for the Widnes district, had, in the course of his duty, to remove a lunatic, named John Heron, to Lancaster Asylum, the other day. Heron preserved a quiet and submissive demeanour until a change of trains was being effected at Hank Quay Station, Warrington. Here, when on the bridge leading from the low level to the high level station, Heron became very violent, and seizing Mr. Scanuell, pushed him with frenzied fury against the side of the passage. The maniac's grip was too firm to be shaken off, and Mr. Scannell's struggles were without avail. At last Heron ran off, making for the centre of the town, by Parker and Sankey-streets, but before he bad proceeded more than 300 yards the relieving officer overtook him, and on this occa- sion obtained the mastery. Heron was dragged back to the railway station, and a request was made for the assistance of the police. Two constables quickly arrived, and Heron was securely handcuffed and bound with straps; and the journey was accomplished without further incident. ASSAULT ON THE POLICE AT RUNCORN.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Michael Kinsey, a respectable looking man, was brought up in custody charged with being drunk and disorderly in Brunswick-street, and also witb assaulting P.C. Kelly.—P.C. Kelly said on the previous night the prisoner was drunk and disorderly in Brunswick- s reet. Witness took him home, but at the expiration of five minutes he rushed from the house and endeavoured to strike a man, but the officer prevented him. The prisoner then tripped the officer, and they both fell to the ground together. The officer took the prisoner to Water-street on the way back to his home, when he turned upon him again, and knocked him to the ground. Teey rolled over each other several times, ani the officer whistled for assistance. P.C. Morris arrived on the scene, and the prisoner was removed to the police station. The prisoner acted like a madman. A man named Brereton assisted the constable, and was kicked in the month by the prisoner.—The prisoner, who pleaded guilty to both charges, was fined 103. and costs for being drunk, and £1 for the assault, or in default six weeks' hard labour.

ALLIGED THEFT BY A RUNCORN BOATMAN. Peter Leather, a boatman, was charged at Runcorn Police Court, on Monday, with stealing two pairs of boots of the value of 128., the property of Joseph Taylor.—The prosecutor is the master of the flat Snafell, and lives at 9. Brook-street, Runcorn ; and the prisoner up to the lit inst. had been as- sisting him to work the vessel. On that day the vessel was lying in the Brunswick dock, Liverpool, and the prisoner without informing the prosecutor went to Runcorn on the flat Hannah. On the sth inst. the prosecutor missed two pairs of shoes from the locker, and subsequently found on the boat a pair of clogs, which he believed belonged to the prisoner. The boots (produced) were owned by the prosecutor.—The prisoner cross-examined the prosecutor to show that he had been lent the shoes; and alleged that he wore them on the fiat for three days.—Ntrs, Taylor stated that the prisoner brought the pair of shoes (preduced ) to her house on Sunday morning. Prisoner at that time denied any knowledge of another pair.—P.C. Bossons deposed to apprehending the prisoner on board a flat on the previous day. When charged the prisoner denied stealing the shoes, and said the prosecutor lent him a pair because he could not lend him money to get his clogs repaired.—The pri- soner was committed to the Quarter Sessions for trial. DANGEROUS ACCIDENT NEAR RUNCORN —A number of the men employed at Camden Soaperv, Runcorn, had a pleasant pic-nic on Sarurd ay. Their wives and friends were of the party, which numbered about 75 persons, and the journey to Pelamere Forest, their destination, was made in conveyances provided by Mr. Peck, who had also obtained a large 'bus drawn by four horses from Mr. Connor, of War- rington. Starting from Deli Bridge at two o'clock, the party had a charming drive, followed by an enjoyable ram- ble in the picturesque woods. In the evening the party returned by way of Toot Hill, and descending the steep gradient the break of the 'bus was applied. Laden with 36 passengers, however, the 'bus seemed to be little restrained by this means, aid the driver's difficulties were added to by the fact that the pole of the vehicle bad snapped. Suddenly the wheels ran into the ditch by the side of the road, and the 'bus was partly overturned, many of the passengers alighting on the top of a thick hedge, while others were pitched over the hedge into the field. After recovering from their alarm, it WAS discovered that none of the passengers were injured, and the pole having been temporarily replaced, the 'bus was driven slowly to Hilton, where the excursionist" were met with conveyances which bad been sent from Runcorn. The party reached home in the small hours of Sunday morn- ing. fortunately no worse off for the untoward incident that had marred the afternoon's proceedings.

SALE OF WORK. In consequence of the conscientious principles of the Bishop of Liverpool, divine service has been conducted in St. Ambrose Churcht, Widnes. for a period of two years without the ceremony of con.secration having been per- formed. The omission of this important part of church thud has been caused in this way. Through lack of funds to carry out the work no boundary wall yet encloses the sacred precincts of the church, and his lordship on prin- ciple declines to consecrate any edifice until it is so fenced in. Although the Building Committee have endeavoured to cotnply with his lordship's expressed wishes, so far they have not succeeded in obtaining sufficient money to justify them in erecting a wall, and hence the uncansecrated, but licensed building Plans of a boundary wall, ornamented with terracotta work, a style harmonious with the handsome church, have, how- ever, been adopted, the estimated cost of the work being £5OO. Mr. Dilworth, contractor, of Wavertree, who was sub-contractor for the church, has been entrusted with the c irryiug out of the designs, and, it is expected, will early set about the erection of the wall. In promises and subscrip- tions £l2O has been obtained towards the expense, and with the object of considerably increasing this amount a sale of work was held in Page-lane Mission-room on Wednesday afternoon. Mr John Brock, J.P., performed the opening c ne•mony. He was supported by the Rev. Geo. Bond, M.A. (vicar of Fern worth), Rev. J. Holden (curate), ' Rev. S. A. Spooner (curate of St. Ambrose), ' Mess 8. E. Carey, Bullough, Valentine, Mercer, Mrs. Biker, Mrs. Neild, Mrs. Pritchard, Miss Rainford, and Miss McLennan. Preparations for the sale had been in pro- gress since November, when the ladies formed a sewing class. Their industrious and facile fingers had produced a large quantity of goods of varied texture and design, which were effectively displayed on the stalls. Elegant articles for the drawing room mingled with more humble housewifery nick- nacks in profusion, although goods of a useful nature were not wanting. The ladies who presided at the stalls were : (1.) Mrs. Menton, Mrs. Valentine, Miss Cooper, Miss Hib- bs,: t ; (2) Mrs. Carey, Miss Meacock, Miss Reintord, Miss Cross, Miss E. Bond , e 3) Mrs. Bond, Mrs. Kershaw, Miss J. Bond, Miss Haddock; (refreshment stall) Mrs. Riley, Mrs. Bullougb, Mrs Pritchard, Mrs. Newton, and Miss Lea. Mr. BROCK said he could assure them it was not his intention to inflict a long speech upon them, but perhaps it might be as well if he addressed a few brief words to those present as to the reason and necessity for this sale of work. It would he within the recollection of mmy there that shortly after the Church of St. Ambrose was opened, a bazaar was held for the purpose of obtaining funds to liquidate a debt which was due to the Building Committee, and also for raising a s.eseof money to be invested as a rep iir fund for the church He was very happy to say that that bazaar held in Novem- ber, 1881, was perfectly satisfactory. They obtained those two objects Shortly after the bezz tr, overtures were made La the Lord Bishop of the diocese with a view to getting the the Church of St. Ambrose consecrated. It was very neces- sary that that ceremony should be performed, especially be. Luse certain church societies, who had promised a sum of money to the building fund would not pay it over until the church had been consecrated. The Bishop m ide many inquiries as to the church, and among other questions he asked was this, "Is there round the church stone fence for protection ? " Unfortunately they were obliged to answer "No." The Bishop at once said that as a matter of principle he could not consecrate the church until a sufficient fence had been provided. He kindly offered to accept a temporary fence, but the committee, after considering this question thoroughly, came to the conclusion that to erect a temporary wooden fence would be a rather foolish expenditure of money, because, as many of them knew, wooden fences in Widues had a happy neck of disap- pearing little by little, during the night time generally, and some fine morning they would have gone to St. Ambrose Church and found the fence gone altogether and their money too. Some delay must, there- fore, unavoidably take place to enable an organi- satioh like that to plan and carry out a project for the raising of a fund to build a wall that should toe a permanent and appropriate fence for the church. That was the object of their We IA Wlrl/4 that dan arii he hoped tbat they would accomplish that object. He was ‘iipoy to siy that they had already some funds in the bank towards the church, and they had promises from numerous sources, and he hoped they might have a suc- cessful sale. (Hear, hear, and applause.) It was very desirable that he money required should be raised immediately in order to obtain the promises from the church societies, which amounted, he thought, to £lOO or £450, and as their 'friends were now commencing to build their church at 'Anderson's Corner that money would be very acceptable I • to their building fund. He need say no more las to the objects of that sale of work, but simply declared the sale open and commit their friends to the tender mercies of the ladies, who were anxious to relieve them of some of that filthy lucre, of which he hoped they had A gooa deal in their possession. (Applause.) The Rev. GrEostGg 'BOND, ALL., tuouglit they ought to thank Mr. Brock, not for the good speech he had made, but for the interest he had displayed in the objects of the sale. It was not the first effort he had made in that direction. From what be could gather—he was not in the neighbour- hood at the time—the success of the late bazaar was owing to Mr. Brock, who laboured diligently in its interest, and placed a MASS of appliances at the disposal of the committee. (Hear, hear.) He had taken great interest in the Church of St. Ambrose, and its present position was a monument to his energy and devotion. (Applause.) The vote of thanks was carried by hearty acclamation. Mr. Bnoce, in reply, said Mr. Bond had spoken in too kind and considerate a manner of the small efforts he had made in connection with St. Ambrose Church. He had taken a great interest in that church, and he did so still. (Applause.) He was thankful to know that there was no debt upon the church, and their efforts with regard to this wall he felt sure would be successful. (Applause.) Tine ladies then proceeded with their sales. The sale was continued on Thursday afternoon. The .otal result was ato ut £lOO.

div.head: RUNCORN BURIAL BO kRII
div.p: RUNCORN BURIAL BO kRII

The monthly meeting was held at the Board-room, Ceme- tery, on Wednesday afternoon. Mr. W. Whittaker presided, and there were present :—Messrs. H. Coleburn, G. Moss, Handley, Win. Littler, and W. F. Salkeld (eecretary).—Mr. HAFDLEY read the financial report, which showed that the month's cash account amounted to £2B 4s, made up as fol- lows :—Fees received, £26 14s: six certificates. £1 103. After the payment of the month's acc iunts, £l4 4s 103 was paid into bank. The Finance Committee recommended the payment of interest, falling due during June, amount- ing to £32 2s ld.—Mr. HANDLEY moved the adoption of the report, and it was seconded by Mr. COLEBURN, who re- marked that the accounts of the Board were in a very satis- factory state. After the cheques of that day had been p.,id there would still be a balance of £134 19s 73 left in the hank.—The minutes were pissid.—The SECRETARY re- ported that the interments in the Cemetery during the two months ending May 25th numbered 60, In the corresponding period of last year 44. The, fees received during those two months amounted to £63 Joe, while in the previous year for' the same period the amount was only £47 15e 2 1 —A. letter was read from Mr. Simkin, dated from 137, Church-street, with reference to lettering the grave stones The writer stated that owing to a pressure of hueiness he had had to en- gage a man to finish some lettering in the Cemetery,he hav- ing asked Ward serveral times to do the work hut could not get him te attend to it.—The SEcagrartv observed that Mr. Simkin had stated that it was not his intention to bring any stranger to do work in the Cemetery—The Board, after some consideration. deemed Mr. Simkin's letter sa.tiefactory. —A communication was read from Mr. Joseph Savage, farmer, with reference to a reduction of the rent of the field adjeinine the Cemetery, which he tenented from the Board He stated that the lend was rented at. too high a sum, con- sidering other land in the neighbourhood —The Board decided to grant a reduciion of £2 per annum, Mr. Savege to do the fencing, the opinion bring express el that the rent was not an exorbitant sum.—The USU ii witice was served on the overseers to call a township meeting on Thursday, the 26th June, for the purpose of appointing three persona as members of the Burial Beard in osc of M. Colehern, Mr. Rhodes, and Mr. Littler, who retire, but are eligible for re-election.

div.head: ASSESSMENT OF WILDERSPOOL BREWERY.
div.p: THE ASSESSMENT OF WILDERSPOOL BREWERY.

A communication from the Assessment Committee was read, stating that they had received notice that the Wilder- spool Brewery Company intend to appear at the Quarter Sessions to appeal against the amount of poor rate assessed on Wilderspool Brewery in March last. The Committee deemed it advisable that they should appear in the name of the Guardians in order that the necessary evidence might be obtained in support of the amount, and they therefore asked for the Board's congest to do so.--Mr. C. REYNOLDS proposed that the Committee have power to take the necessary steps in the matter.—The CHAIRMAN sad he believed that according to the Parliamentary returns the brewers were receiving less . profits than they were formerly. —Mr. REYNOLDS said he thought the Committee took no notice ot the profits that were being gained. They did not assess on the profi:s but on the DAaßvsmucexpressed his confidence in the Committee.—Mr. IANNua seconded the motion, and it was carried.

div.head: SEWERAGE WORKS.
div.p: THE SEWERAGE WORKS.
The CLERK intimated that he had received the draft of lease for the land required for the suwerage works ; and it was referred to tha Sanitary Cominittee.
FINANCE.
Accounts amounting to £1,252 7s 81 were read and passed for payment, lu the motion of Mr. HANDLEY, seconded by Mr. LOCKWOOD.
ELECTIONS OF OILLEIDIANS.

A circular was read from the Swansea Union trusting that the Board would adopt a similar memorial to the one adopted by the Swansea Union respecting the voting at the elections of Guardians, and sent by them to the Local Government Board. A copy of the memorial accompanied the circular, from which it appeared that the meinorialists called attention to the three systems of voting which exist in the election of town councils, school boards, and boards of guardians, the two former ef which are by ballot and the latter by voting papers. It went on to say that the three distinct methods of voting—crosses in one case, figures in another, and initials in another—led to confusion, and were the cause of a large number of votes being lost, being in- valid in consequence of being improperly tilled üb. That elections of tivardians should Da by ballot, the existing system of voting papers being a bad one. That town coun- cil, school board, and guardian elections should be held at the same time and place as nearly as practicable for the convenience of voters and to save expense. The memo- rialists prayed that the Local Government Board would cause to be introduced before the Houeeof Commons a bill to carry out the foregoing alterations in the law.—Mr HANDLEY proposed that the Board assent to a memorial similar to the one referred to.—Mr. CILALLONER seconded the pro- position. He thought they had had smuggling long enough. —The CLERK pointed out that the machinery of the ballot would be much more expensive then that of the voting papers.—Mr. HANDLEY said they had four elections in Run- corn, and be thought if they were all taken at the same time they would be no more expensive than at present.—Mr. MCINTYRE said he was an advocate of the ballot if they could have it at the same price. He had in his hand a re- turn of the two systems as exercised in Runcorn. The election of the School Board by ballot cost £ll9 14s, and the election of the Guardians by voting papers cost £32 9s Bd. Whitley happened to have a School Board, and the cost of the election was £l9 23 61, while the cost of the election of Guardians was £2 14s. The sixpenny loaf in one case would cost 2s in the other. If he could have a guarantee that they should have the sixpenny loaf for sixpence he would vote for the ballot, but he certainly would alt like to see them involved in a COnteet which cost nine times more than lhe Present method.—The c''.3.Cltign W $lO, 'Would the ballet, if granted, be compul- sory in every township? to which the CLERK replied in the neirative.—Mr. CHALLONER described the voting paper system as a "jumbled up concer9," and said that intimida- tion had been used in order to secure the election of mein- bars.—Sir. MCINTYRE said he never knew a case of intimi- dation in the election of a member of that Board, but if it could be proved to his satisfaction that there had been such a thing either by landlords, employers, or tradesmen, he would vote for the ballot.—Mr. CHALLONER renewed his assertion that intimidation had been practiced, and said he ' was of opinion that it had been carried on throughout the Union.—On the motion being put, nine voted for and five against it. This was all the business of public interest.

RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY. The fortnightly meeting of this Authority was held on Tuesday, at Dutton Workhouse. There were present—The Keys. Canon Barclay (chairman), J. W. N. Tanner, and John Lockwood; Messrs. John Ashton, J. Mclntyre, John Weir, J. Knowles, W. Whitlow, J. Darbyshire, W. Jackson. T. Andrews, J. Challoner, J. Highfield, H. Stringer, 11. Linaker (clerk), W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk), and J. Farrington (inspector). THE WORKING OF THE CANAL BOATS' Acr. Mr. FARRINGTON presented the following report resp,=ct- ing the working of the Canal Boats' Act in the district of the , Authority i—Although there is a very long length of canals within the rural sanitary district of the Runcorn Union there is no terminus, consequently only one wide boat has been registered by the Authority, the accommodation being for four persons in after-cabin. The inspection of boats plying on the various canals within the district of the Sani- tary Authority is undertaken and carried out by the inspector of nuisances, the result being that overcrowding has greatly diminished and the boats are kept much cleaner. Since August, 1879, being the time the Sanitary Authority has been constituted a registration authority, pro- ceeding,s have been taken in 37 instances, and.a conviction obtained in each, as will be seen from the following sum- mary :—Proceedings taken under section one, 17; amount of fines and costs, £l2 123. Proceedings taken under sec- tion two, 14; amount of fines and costs, £9 13s. 101 Pro- ceedings taken under section three, 6; amount of fines and costs, £4 9s. The Education Act will always to a large extent be evaded by the canal population so long as nar- row boats are worked in pairs. Overcrowding will exist 1 until it is compulsory for all inspectors of nuisances to de- vote some portion of their time to the inspection of boats through their districts.—The report was adopted.

THE ANCROBUS WELL. The Depoty Clerk laid before the Board the copy of a letter sent by him to Messrs Simpson and Hackin, solicitors, asking if Mr. Holt would allow an inspection of the plan and conveyance of the property, to which he had received the following reply :—" 9, Mount-street. Albert-square, Man- chester, Mb June, 1883.—Dear Sir,—We sent a copy of your letter of the 411 instant to our client, Mr. IN in. Holt, of this city, who has to-day seen us upon the matter. He declines to produce any documents or give any information whatever, except at the cost in all respects of your clients. We must say that we agree with him that this is only fair, as the point raised by Mr. Farringtot was raised about six years ago, and such explanation was then given as we thought bad settled the matter. Upon hearing from you that you wish us to make a search for the papers, and upon receiving your undertaking to pay our oosts we will look in- to the matter so as to be able to communicate more folly with you. Yours truly, SIMPSON AND HAGRIN."—The Board, after a short conversation, instructed the clerk to re- ply to the solicitors that the Authority were satisfied the well was public property, and unless it was opened forth- with steps would be taken to have it opened.

HALTON DRAINAGB. Mr. C. L. Evans, agent to Sir Richard Brooke, Bart., wrote the inthority stating that with regard to the way- leave of 77 yards through land belonging to Sir Richard Broske. the litter gentleman was willing to grant permission for such wayleave provided that compensation be paid to the present tenant for surface damage and also to any future tenant, and that au agreement to this effect be drawn up and a tracing attached ---The Board: gave: instructions for the agreement to he prepared in accprdance with the terms of Mr. Evans' letter.

div.head: RUNCORN CONSERVATIVE ASSOCIATION.

There were present, amongst others, the Revs Canon B trclay, M.A., W. Preston. M.A., J. Lockwood, BA; Messrs. W. Whittaker, C. R. H. Harrison, J. K. Digges, W. H. Rogerson. W. Farrell, and J. W. Lighhurn (secretary). The statement was odoptgd, arid the "Meeting proceeded to elect officers. • Sir Richard Brooke, But, was re-elected president of the asso- Ir, elation , Mr..,J. Brundrit, J.P., chairman; Dr. Stirle, ch eir _tnan a n mittees ; and Mr. W. Whittaker, treasurer. The committel was substantially the same as that of last year. The foliowlog gentlemen were elected vice-presidents en bloc: Revs:Canon Berclay, M.A., W. Preston, M.A.. J. Lockwood; and J. J. Bryant, MA.' Mr. R. M. Brooke, J.P., Mr. W. Wright. J.P., Mr. S. B. Chadwick, J.P.. Mr. H. Reynolds, J.P., Mr. W. Bankes J.P., Mr. A. Thomas, J.P., Capt. Hezlehurst, J.P., Mr. Chas. Wigg, Mr. W. Haves, Dr. Steele, Dr. Mouritz, Mr. G. L. Wiv, and Dr. Carruthers. Votes of thinks were unanimously accorded to Sir Richard Brooke, Bert., and Major Orred for their liberal donations to the funds of the society, and also to the former for his ser- vices. Mr. Brundrit (chairtnan of the association), Dr. Steele (chairmen of committees), Mr. Whittaker (treasurer), and J. W. Lightburn (Secretary), were each thanked for their services. Mr. Lightburn, in replying, said be thought the fact that the Runcorn polling district had polled a greater per centage of voters than any other part of that division of +he c iuntv was creditable alike to the association and their ~ppiments. The usual complim,nt having been paid the chairman, the meeting concluded.

div.head: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board witi held on Thurs- day, the metnbers preient being Mr. W. Tyrer (chairman), Rev. T. Finegan, Messrs. Fidler, Meadows, Marsh, Loather. barrow, Hall, Buckley, Gil body, P. Longton, Matthews, Sad- ler, Syder, Gerrard, Criffiths, Ashton, Hulme, Kenwright, Agnew, r•ol,ell

ATIPOINTMENTS. A letter was read from the Local Government Board sanctioning the appointment of Mr. Henry A. Twist as assistant overseer of Windle at sixpence in the pound on the amount collected. The master and matron (Mr. and Mrs. ! Bicknell) wrote drawing attention to the amount of their salaries, and the arduous nature of their duties, and requesting the appointment of an assistant matron. The matter was referred to the Visiting Committee. Letters were read from Mr. Scinnell, relieving officer for Widnes, asking for a testimonial in sup- port of his application for the mastership of Barrow Work- house, and from Mr. Bullock, one of the relieving officers for Sr. Helens, for a testimonial in supp)rt of the relieving officership of another township. The letters were referred the clerk.—in pursuance of notice, Mr. HALL moved that Mr. George LATI imer, the master's clerk, be granted a super- annuation allowance of £2O a year.—Mr. FIDLER seconded the motion, and it was carried unanimously.

TES ADDITOR AGAIN. The CLERK stated that since last meeting Mr. Haxlehurst had ttought fit te send one of his clerks into the district to audit the relieving officers' books. The auditor had thought 'fit to make certain reports with regard to the relievinir offi.iers' accounts, the correctness of which reports he (the clerk) had felt it his duty to deny, and he had written to Mr. Hazlehurst pointing out the gross irregularity of send- ing down his clerk to examine the books after closing the audit. He asked the Board to pass a resolution that the books should riot be inspected except at the times prescribed by law. It had already been decided in a court of law that an auditor had no right to re-open accounts, more especially when he did so en order to bolster up an incorrect report sent by him to the • Local Government Board.—Mr. LEATREBBARROW had great pleasure in moving the resolu- tion suggested by Mr. Hartley.—Mr. HALL seconded the motion, with the addition that copies of the resolution be sent to the auditor, the Local Government Board, and the relievini. officers. He regarded the action of the auditor as a very great injustice to their clerk, who did his work faithfully. It was very unfair indeed, very undignified, and a very unkind and im- proper thing.--Mr. FIDLER : I go further. I think the auditor's conduct engenders suspicion between the clerk and the relieving officers, and I move that we ask for a commission to c4neider his conduct and to curb his un- official officiousness.—Mr. NEWSOME seconded the motion. remarking that a ream capable of such mean, low conduct was not fit for his post.— Mr. FIDLEw. said that their work for the last twelve or eighteen months had been nothing but the auditor.—The Cuentetere : He has increased our rates. —Mt. FIDLER :He has increased our annoyances. But there is one consolation, that he does the same in every j Union he goes into.—After some conversation, Mr. Fidler withdrew his motion, and that of Mr. Leatherbarrow was agreed to.

div.head: INFECTIOUS DISEASES.
div.p: INFECTIOUS DISEASES.

Rev. T. FINEGAN asked for a return showing the number of cases of infectious diseases sent iuto the workhouse hospital in the last month.—The CLnaz promised to furnish the return in a day or two. div.head: LATEST
div.p: LATEST

The appointment of Lord Dufferin to the tirand k,rues of the Bath was gaz,tted last night. In the chess tournament yerterday morning, Mortimer beat Zakertort, Mackenzie beat Winawer, and Eoglische beat Noah. _ _ _

Henry Cornforth, a wiredrawer, of Manchester, was drow_led in Hollingworth Lake on Thursday night, by a pleasure boat capsizing. His companion was saved. A petition for liquidation has been presented in the Lon- don Bankruptcy Court by Emanuel Moritz, merchant, of Bury-street, St. Mary Axe, the liabilities being stated at £30,000. The assets are valued at £lB,OOO. Sir John Savage, formerly Mayor of Belfast, after baying wounded his neck in a shocking manner, died yesterday morning. The suicide is said to have been without motive and is therefore attributed to a fit of insanity. At Asliton-under-Lyne, on Thursday night, one of four children of an overlooker named Bottointey was found quite dead, suspended from the iron framework of a bad- stead, in which she must have become entangled whilst play- ing. The other children were found sleeping quietly. It having been determined to revive the Lady Liodiva pro- cession this year through the streets of the city of Coventry, steps are being taken for carrying out the project. The mayor has agreed to grant the use of the ancient armour in St. Mary's Hall, and it is intended that the pageant shall surpass in magnificence those of former times. A private meeting a Limeri o.k Corporation, held on Thursday, for the purpose of drafting an address to the Lord Lieutenant on his forthcoming visit, was of a most stormy character. Nationalists proposed paragraphs relat- ing to Home Rule, Clifford Lloyd, etc., and great uproar ensued, which could be heard in the streets. The Accrington police report the terrible death of a child. During the night-time the wife of a lab mrer named Nuttall administered some vitriol instead of limswater to her child aged under two years. Ihe child screamed and appeared to be suffering great pain, and on the father tasting the contents of the bottle he found out the mistake. The child, whose mouth was badly burnt, died a few hours afterwards. Yesterday morning a furniture broker named Taylor, of King-street, Oldham, was horrified on entering his shop to discover the lifeless body of Richard Hoyle, who had been occasionally employed by him. The deceased was formerly employed at the Oldham Infirmary, but latterly haying ir- regular employment, became addicted to intemperance, and generally neglected himself. Yesterday morning a fire broke out at the residence of the Right Hon. Lord Ribblesdale, of Gisburn. The fire originated in the lady's-maid's room, through the over- heating of a flue. A telegram was despatched to Clitheroe for assistance, and the steam fire enaine came, bat the fire was got under before it arrived, and before much damage was done. 'I he damage is covered by insurance. The last of the Irish families have left Turton, near Damen, as requested by the English section of the inhabi- tants. There was ne demonstration made, though large crowds assembled, the Irish taking their expulsion quietly. Some thirty families have been ejected. At one house twenty-eight persona were trained out, but these included lodgers. There is not a single Irishman or woman now in the town.

THE MURDER OF LORD MOTINTMORRIS : A SOLDIER APPROVER. Tom Higgins, a soldier, and supposed approver, arrived at Cong, on Thursday night, under a strong escort of police, to be examined as a witness, under the Crimes Act, in con- n.ction with Os murder of Lord Mountmorris. Higgins was fcrmerly a servant boy in Clonbur at the time of the assassination, and on one occasion he received a month's imprisonment for a violent aesault committed on a Boycotted police-car driver. ALLEGE, D WIFE MURDER AT LIVERPOOL. At Liverpool to-day, Robert Arthur Holt was charged with causing the death of his wife, who was found dead ender mysterious circumstances in their house, having been stabbed in the neck with a table knife. The prisoner's story was that the woman fell on the knife. Medical evidence was given to the effrct that the wourd could not have been self-inflicted, but inlet have been caused by,somebody else. The prisoner, who reserved his defence, was committed to the assizes on the charge of wilful murder. DARING ROBBERS AT LIVERPOOL. A policeman on duty in lelington, Liverpool, early yester. day morning, discovered dangling from the second storey window of a temperance hotel a rope formed of bed-cloth- ing knotted together. The police-officer aroused the in- mates, when it was discovered that a woman who had been sleeping in the house had disappeared, having rifled the pockets of a gentleman also staving in the house, stealing his watch, money, and other Yalu thlea. The woman then entered an unoccupied room, and tying an improvised rope to the bedpost escaped by that means. THE 11e.NDEL FEiTIVA.L. The rehearsal for the eighth triennial Handel festival took place yesterday, at the Crystal Palac,, and, as is cus- tomary, c nisisted of extracts from various works, which will he performed on the three days of the festival itself. Mr. August Manna, in the absence, through iudisposition of Michael Costa, conducted, and will do so throughout. The chief features of the choral singing yesterd tv, were the fine rendering of choruses "When His loud voice," from "Jeptha ;" " Davy," from "Saul ;" " Hallelujah," from the " Messiah ;" " Wretched lovers." from " Acis and Gallatea," and various choruses from "Israel." The chief instrumental item was the concerts for organ and orchestra• number one. The organ in this was magnificently played by Mr. W. T. Best, of Liverpool, wile introduced a very fine cadenza, which was much applauded. The soloists were Mesdames Patey, Vallerin, and Trebelli ; Messrs. Santiey and Barton McGucken. The rehearsal was very satisfactory, and augurs well for the success of the forth- coming festival. The members present were 16,873, against 11,448 on rehearsal day in 1880.
FATAL FIRE IN SCOTLAND. FOUR PERSONS BURNED TO DEATH.

An alarming fire broke out shortly after midnight on Thursday at a warehouse in Inglis-street, Inverness, which caused ,the death of at least four persons The street in which the fire broke out is situated within 300 yards of the railway station, to the left of the Station Hotel, a thickly populated but comparatively poor locality. The fire was first observed an hour after the inmates had retired, and the flames had made considerable progress when the alarm was raised. The scene then witnessed was one without parallel in its horror so far as the highland elpit4l is concerned. The poor people—men, women, and children—rushed wildly from the burning building with nothing but their night- dress on, and some even without as much to cover them. Their cries of terror were painfnl. Such was the nature of the building that there was little time left for rescuing any of the inmates. Fifteen, however, managed to escape, but four pe,ished miserably, their means of escape being cut off. These were a pensioner named Ferguson, his wife, and two children, their nieces, who had been living with them. It is believed that but for their heroic endeavours to save the children, Ferguson and his wife would have escaped. Their sad fate has caused a thrill of horror in the district, where Ferguson was well known. Several persons sustained ight injuries, but it was at first believed that the list of persons burned to death would be increased when the names were known. Inquiries have, however, elicited that this is happily the whole number. The origin of the fire is unknown. The facilities for extinguishing fire In In- verness are very inadequate, and the brigade appliances are not yet in "workicg order. The danger of this state of things was fully demonstrated yesterday.

div.head: BRIGFIr CELEBRATION.
div.p: THE BRIGFIr CELEBRATION.

Mr. Bright was entertained at breakfast by the Mayor. of Birmingham, yesterday morning, and referring to the pro- posed second Suez Canal, he advised England to go had in hand with France in making it. Great national interests were at stake, and the concord between two great nations. Where India was concerned, men seemed to lose their heads, but be hoped that with regard to the canal it might be dis- cussed in a cool and sober manner. Then, as to the proposed Channel Tunnel, it would be a great benefit to England and France if it could be successfully accomplished. He ridiculed the fears of invasion which hut been shown by military authorities, and said that those who talked about Dyer being taken, with the country ten miles round it, were only fii" for Bediam. It the tunnel were made, it would be of enormnns value to this country, and to Europe generally. He hoped the ab- surd, monstrous, inconceivable suggestion would be utterly disregarded and repudiated by the common seri% of our countrymen. As Lord Derby had said, the greatest interest of this country was peace, and anything which could ba done to promote it—such as furthering the means of com- munication between nations—should be supported by the people, as be hoped would be the case in the present in- stance.

Mr. Bright subsequently unveiled the statue of Wright, who was elected member for Nottingham, but die 4 ' suddenly without taking his seat. A meeting was held afterwards in the Town Hal!, at which Mr. Bri;..;.t, sai4 that Mr. Wright was a specimen of those men of 'lrhotn there were so many throughout the country, ,sho, were willing to promote the intellectual advancement of, and every kind of good amongst, the poorer classes of the com- munity.

ORDER OF BUSINESS —Mr. GLADSTONE said it being tho prevailing &sire of the House, the Corrupt Practices Bill would be proceeded with in the Commons without interruptions to its close; and after that the Tenants' Compensation Bill would be taken. This determination had been come to not with the desire of impeding the passing of either Bill, but to facilitate the progress of both. Tag Connurr PRACTICES BILL —The House went into committee on the Corrupt Practices Bill. Clause 2, defining what was corrupt practice, was under clnsideration. By leave, Mr. PARNELL withdrew the amendment he submitted last night, and moved another in different words, but almost to the same effect, to prevent force, violence, restraints damage, injury, harm, abduction, duress, or fraudulent con- trivance; to be put on voter prior to giving his vote.—The ATTORNEY GENERAL could not accept the amendment. He was willing that the effect of the Act of 1854 should be the same in Ireland as it was in England and Scotland.—Mr. FOWLER regretted the determination of the Attorney General. The member for Cork had proposed to insert the whole of the enactment of the Act of 1834 in the Bill, ex- cept the words, "or in any other manner practiced intimida- tion." The real question was, were they prepared to pre- vent Roman Catholic clergymen exercising influence over tbe voters, by rendering them liable for making a speech at an election in favour of a particular candidate to imprison- ment for 12 months. He asked the committee whether, 'in the present situation of Ireland, they were pre- pared to endorse such a statement. He hoped Mr. Parnell would press his amendment, and that it would be supported by the Liberal party.— Sir C. DILKE said Mr. Justice Fitzgerald had laid it (lowa how far a Roman Catholic clergyman could go on the sub- . ject. Bill he (Sir C. I GENERAL could not, on the part of the Government, accept the amendment, and thereby allow undue spiritual influence to remain unchecked in Ireland.—Mr. PARNELL said he. GENERAL, as a concession. slid if Mr. Parnell withdrew hig amendment he would undertake to bring up a new clause dealing with undue spiritual influence.—Mr. PARNELL said he would consent if the proposal was brought up as subsec- tion to the clause that would prevent the matter now under consideration being deferred until they came to deal with new clauses.—Sir R. rnoss said he would reserve his altera- tion in the motion until he saw the Government proposal on paper.—The ATTORNEY-GENERAL would do his best to SA hie proposal on paper by Monday.—Mr. Parnell's amend- ment Was then withdrawn—Verbal amendments were ac- cepted from M. PERSONATING FEMALES IN LIVER-
POOL. EXTRAORDIFARY REVELATIONS,

A strange and somewhat amusing case was revealed to the Liverpoal police on Thursday, the partinlars of which are as follow :—lt appears that late on Tnesday night, whilst a Sheffield gentleman was standing outside the Royal Court Theatre, a young "lady," mo'st stylishly attired, came up. to him, and entered into a conversttion, in the caurSe of which the fair stranger abruptly left him, and ran down John's-lane. The gentleman immediately missed his gold breastpin, which was valued at £3, and at once gave cbasa to the supposed thief, following her down John's-lane, up Manchester-street, and into a street off Date-street known as North-street. Here the woman waa•stopped by a police. constable, 401, who, believing there was something wrong took her to the Detective Office. The gentleman intryiediately,came up and explained matters to the officer, who subsequen/ly ptonured'alight;Jand, 'lliegulaily enough, fond the gold-pin on the pavement in North-street, close 4: the spot where he had stopped ,the thief, Ttie yonog "woman " was 'at once given into custody, and apared before Mr. Raffles, the stipendiary magistrtte, on Wed- nesday morning, on a charge of haying stolen the pin, and after evidence had been called the prisoner, who gave the name of “Sarah Cuckwell," pleaded guilty. Mr. }Wiles re- , marking that he had only one sentencu for snob characters, ' who went about ostensibly for the purpOse of robhing men, and he would therefore sentence her to six months' imprison- ment. Prisoner was then removed, and subsrquently non-__ veyed to Walton Gaol, but it appears that soon after arriv- ing there, and when about being placed :dung with other female prisoners, she called the female warder aside and hinted that they were Placing her h r t ine namethe wrongo f H epnarryt of o the. hk gaol, as she was a man, d gave Cock- well. A doctor was immediately called in, Who shortly afterwards corroborated the statement of the prisoner.

SCHOOL SERMONS AT STUI:SHAW CROSS.—The annual school sermons in connection with St. Luke's Mission Church at Stubshaw. Cross, Ashton, were preached on Sun. day, and collections were made in aid of the Sunday Schools, The Rev. W. F. Lovell, M.A. of Newton, preached in the afternoon, and in the evening the pulpit was occupied t‘y the Rev. Canon Dodd, of Stretton. The sum of £4 5s 21 was raised.

GAR.AVOOD HALL COLLIERIES ANNUAL TRIP.—The annual trip in connection with the Garswood Hall Colliery of Messrs. Smethurst, Hoyle and Grime, took place on Mon- day last, and was in every respsct a decided success. The destination was Blackpool, "The Brighton of the North," , and about 700 persons were conveyed thereto. The train left Brynn Station at 6 o'clock, and proceeded via Wigan. As the day was brilliantly fine, everyone enjoyed them- selves, and arrived safe home about ten o'clock the same evening. I.IIE SAVAGE WIFE ASSAULT AT ASIITON.—At the Wigan County Police Court, on Friday, Christmas Evans, a Welshman, living at Ashton, was charged on remand with assaulting his wife, Lydia Evans, on Tuesday morning.— Complainant said that on Monday night her husband brought a man home with him, and allowed him to stay all night. On Tuesday morning the two Uleß went out to- gether, and on prisoner returning he fastened the doors and came upstairs and passed her bedroom. In a minute or two he entered her room with a pick-shaft, and on asking him what he was going to do, he said he would let her know and make her remember being drunk the day before. Prisoner then beat her with the pick-shaft all over her body. Wit- ness called out for assistance, and her husband struck her across the face, and went out of the house leaving her for dead.—ln answer to the prisoner, witness said she was drunk on Monday morning when she paid her shop bill, but her husband had beaten her before the assault complained of was committed. Mrs. Brown, of Crippin's- buildings, Ashton, deposed that between eight and nine o'clock on Tuesday prisoner came to her house and said, "What does ta think I have done? I have made yonder -- so that she c nanot get up. I beat her with a pick arm." Witness went to prisoner's house and found the woman in a very weak state and much bruised. Police-constable , M'Phail stated that when he apprehended the prisoner and charged him with the assault, he answered: "I was working on Monday and I left money with my wife to pay the shop bill. When I came home she was drunk, and what I have done I did it in 9. passion, and I am very sorry for it."—Dr. Hannah said that he had examined the complainant. She ' had been very much abused, and had several severe wounds all over her body.— Prisoner acknowledged the assault and expressed his sorrow for what lie had done. It was because of her getting drunk that he had beaten her, and if the Bench would be merciful with him he would never abuse her again. —The Bench committed prisoner to gaol for two calendar months with hard labour.

div.head: CROFT.
div.p: CROFT.

CHOIR PARTY AT CRC/FT.—On Saturday afternoon, the members of the choir of Christ Church, Croft, and a few friends, to the number of 34, were entertained at the Rectory by the Rev. T. P. and Mrs. Kirkman. About five o'clock the pirty sat down to a substantial tea, presided over by Mrs. Sherlock and Miss Kirkman, after which various games were indulged in until half-past nine o'clock. Supper was then provided, and after having given hearty cheers for Mr., Mrs., and Miss Kirkman, Mrs. Sherlock, and others for their kindness, the National Anthem was sung, and the party broke up, having spent a very pleasant evening. ANNIVERSARY SERMONS AT THE UNITARIAN CHAPEL, LADY-LANE.—On Sunday two sermons were preached in the above chapel by the Rw. W. C. Squlrer, of Stand, in aid of the Sunday Schools. The services both afternoon and even- ing were crowded, many people being unable to gain admit- tance. Special hymns appropriate to the occasion were sung by the choir. The collections amounted to about £lB.---- The annual tea party for the scholars, teachers, and friends, in connection with the above place of worship took place on Monday afternoon, when about 80 persons sat down to a substantial tea provided in the schoolroom, after which they adjourned to a field kindly lent by Mr. Thomas Welsby, where various games were indulged in until about ten o'clock, when the party broke up, all being highly pleased with their afternoon's enjoyment. Nuts, sweets, d:c, were distributed amongst the scholars during the evening.

LOWTON PARISH CHURCH SCHOOLS ANNUAL SERMONS. —Three special sermons were preached in Lowtou Church on Sunday last, the occasion being the anniversary services in connection with the day and Sunday schools. The morning and evening preacher was the Rev. J. Coombes, vicar of St. Paul's Church, Portwood, near Stockport; and the afternoon preacher was the Bev. W. Smith, vicar of Christ Church, Pennington. The services were marked with special hymns and anthems by the school children and choir, and in every way they were successful, nearly £4O being collected.
