A letter from the Golborne Liberal Association also complaining of the high price charged for the water was left over until the next meeting.—The Serj Tay,k; : Mr. Garton , moved, and Mr. Pierpoint seconded, that the I work recommended by the Highway and Sewerage Committee at the sewage tanks, to the effect that the filters be cleaned out and replen- ished with fresh material periodically, and that endeavours he made to purify the sewage as much as pos- sible before admitting it it into the brook, be carried out.— An A'leged Nteisance.—On the motion of Mr. J. HALE.

ALARMING F/Rll.—About half-past three on Tuesday afternoon a house in Town Road, Hale, occupied by Wil- liam Hughes and Edward Torten, was discovered to be on fire by Turton's daughter. She at once sent to the fire- engine station, which is near the house in question, and Sergeant-Instructor Price, with 18 firemen, hastened to the spot. An effort was made to remove the furniture from the burning house, and this was successfully carried out, with- out any serious damage being done to the goods. There was a stiff breeze at the time, and It was feared that the flames might spread to Colonel Mewlaurn's stable, which stands in close proximity* the scene of the fire. Water was ob- tained from a pit about 900 yards away at Houghton Towers, and water-carts, barrels, and various other vessels were brought into requisition in order to convey it to the burning house. P.S. Coulter and P.C. Roberts soon arrived oh the scene, and, in conjunction with the firemen, did their utmost to get the flames under. The house was a thatched one, and the roof, dry as tinder, was licked up with incredNe swiftness by the flames. By half-past six the fire had been extinguished—not, however, barons the house bad been completely wrecked. The occur- rence is supposed to have been caused by Ellen Turton put- ting two or three pieces of wood on the fire about three o'clock in the afternoen. Owing to this circumstance the chimney was fired, and the sparks falling on the thatched roof, the whole building was enveloped in flames before any- thing could be done to stay their progress. The fire origin- ated in that part of the house occupied by Turton. The damage is estimated at £l3O, which was covered by insurance in the Royal Fire and Life Insurance Company, Liverpool. The furniture was not insured.

The preacher in the afternoon and evening was the Rev. W. Inman. of St. Helens; Mr. J. Woods, of Earle& town, delivering an excellent address in the morning. Selec- •tions of music were rendered by the choir of the Earlestown Primitive Chapel, and special hymns were sung by the sehulars. The collections were in aid of the Sunday school funds, arid the sum of 15s was realised. THE RECENT GRANTING OF A SEPARATION ORDER: 4INGHL4R,APPLIcATioN.—A sotnewhat singular application was made at the Neon Petty Sessions, on; t_4aturday last. •'the magistrates en the. Bench were George McOorqecqlale, Hon;hton, and C." -Pilkington,"Esq-a—Mr: Moore, solici- tor, of .Warrimeron, said he had; subj..** notice already served, to apply for the r eluetion of anAteder of 7s; ed. per week to 3s, per week, whic!l was made on John Heaton on the 28th April last. On the 31st March the man named was brought before the magistrates on a summons by his l•wife, and was fined 403. and costs for assaulting her. Nailing at all was said about a separation order at that time, but subsequently Mr. Knowles appeared before the curt and asked for a separation order, which was granted. The defendant, however, could not really afford to pay 7s. ed. per week. He was not at the time profes- sionally represented, or an order for that amount might not have been granted. The defendant's ' wife was his seemed wife and she had had no children ty him. By his first wife he had seven children

left him, and four of these he had to keep himself. Hs was really not in a position to pay is. 6d. per week towards his wife, and he (Mr. Moore) thous;ht lithe circumstances had been properly explained to their worships they would never have made the order so heavy. It was only in cases of judicial separation where the wife had had children by her husband that so large an order was made, and as it was not so in that case he asked that the order might be Mr. Knowles appeared for the wife and submitted that the Bench had no jurisdiction in the case, as the only ground upon which his friend could base his application was that the circumstances of the defendant were changed since the case was heard. That had not been shown and he sub- mitted that the case could not go any further.—Mr. Moore thought there had been a change in the position of the affairs of the defendant since the order was made, because the whole of the four children were now dependent upon him.—Mr. White (deputy clerk) pointed out that there had been no change in that respect since the order was made, and the Bench declined to make any alteration in the order. HUYTON QUARRY.

CLAIM AGRINST THE LONDON AND NORTH-WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.—At the St. Helens County Court on Saturday—before Mr. T. P. E. 1 hompson, judge—a claim was brought by Wm. Magnus, of Huyton Quarry, to recover from the London and North-Western Railway Company the sum of £7 Hs Bd, 133 8d of which was for damage to furni- ture, and bad been paid into cour thy the company. The amount which, therefore, remained disputed, was £7 33 for damage done to china in removal.—A jury was empanelled.— Mr. J. 0. Swift appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. Preston defended.—lt appeared that the plaintiff, prior to February last, lived at Okengates, Shropshire, but having obtained a better situation at the ironworks at Huyton Quarry, he re- moved there. Previous to doing this he went to the station master at Okengates and spoke to him about the removal of the furniture, &c., and told him to be very careful with three barrels, one crate, one large box, and one small box, in which were packed about £5O worth of china. On these reaching Huyton Station, however, it was found that some of the china in the small box and one of the barrels had been broken, the damage being estimated at the sum claimed by Mr. Riley, of Liverpool, a dealer in china, tic. It was pointed out by Mr. Swift that if the contents of the box and barrel in which the breakage had occurred had sepa- rately been worth more than £lO the defendants would not be liable, according to Act of Parliament, as no special rate of insurance had been paid on the boxes; but he con- tended that the contents of neither of these parcels had been separately worth £lO, and called several witnesses who supported this statement. He also called witnesses who spoke to the careful way in which che china had been packed, and the care which had been taken of it whilst in the hands of the plaintiff.—On the other hand, no witnesses were called on behalf of the defence, but Mt. Preston re- marked upon the probability there was of the contents of the two packages being separately worth more than £lO, as they were admitted to contain the most valuable of time china, and also referred to the likelihood there was of their being badly packed.—His Honour, in directing the jury, drew attention to the fact that the witnesses were all for one side, and said that witnesses might have also been called for the defence if the defendants had thought it likely that they would support their case.—A verdict for the full amount with costs was given.

div.p: LYMM.

A COAL DEALER AND HIS SCALE.—MAIIIICIV Thorny croft, coal dealer, of Lymm, was summoned at Lymm Petty Sessions, yesterday, charged with having in his pos- session a certain scale which was false.—lt appeared that on the 6th instant defendant's coal yard was visited by a police- constable, who discovered a quantity of iron and wood attached to one end of the scale, but not permanently secured to it. The scale was jut so long as the iron and wood was attached, but when that was taken off the scale was found to be nibs. against the purchaser.—Defendant said the scale was only in temporary use, his other scale having been sent for repairs, and he attached the iron and wood in order to make it just, as he did not wish to be considered a rogue "for the sake of a lump of coal."—The Bench said he bad broken the law in not having his scale right, but they did not think he had been cheating the public. He would be fined ss. and costs 12s. 6d.

CRUELTY TO A DOG AT LYMII. - Yesterday, at Lymm Petty Sessions, a labourer, named Walter Boond, of Lvmm, was summoned on a charge of haying cruelly tortured and ill-treated a dog, belonging to Mrs. Rawson, also of Lymm. —lnspector Harper, of the S.P.C.A., appeared to prosecute, and Mr. T. Addenbrook, of Warrington, appeared for the defendant, who pleaded not guilty.—lt appeared that on the 25th ult., Jesse Rawson, a young man, son of Mrs. Rawson, was walking out near the Spread Eagle in company with another young man, named Ernest Ardern, and the dog, which was after the collie breed, was following them. When near to defendant's house' which is close to the Spread Eagle, a spaniel dog belonging to Mr. Crostield, the defendant's employer, commenced fighting with the collie. Rawson as soon as he found an opportunity parted them, pulling his dog away by the tail; and defendant, who had heard the dogs fighting, ran out of his house with a broom and went to Rawson's dog and struck it on the head with the broom. The dog fell senseless to the ground and it was car- ried into the yard of the Spread Eagle. Mr. Entwhistle, veterinary sargeon, was called, and found the dog's head dreadfully bruised, the frontal bone being broken. Stimu- lants wore administered, and the dog partially recovered consciousness, but it appeared to be in great agony and howled so frantically that it was considered advisable to destroy it, and this was done by means of poison.—The defence set up by Mr. Addenbrook was that complainant's dog being a vicious one and in the habit of fighting with other dogs it met in the street, defendant was justified in striking it in defence of his master's property, his master's dog having followed him home from work.—The bench said they did not think defendant had wilfully tortured the dog, bat he was guilty of very hasty conduct. He 'would te fined ss, and costs 325. NANTWICH.

AN EXTRAORDINARY CASR.—Mr. Thomas Hughes, county court judge, was occupied until a late hour on Wednesday evening, at Nantwich, adjudicating upon an extraordinary claim made by Mr. John Cooper, a well-known gentleman in Nantwich, against his late groom, Mottram. The action was brought to recover a mare or its value, £3O, as well as £4 belonging to the plaintiff. Mrs. Cooper was accustomed to hunt with the Cheshire hounds, and on the 29th Decem- ber she met her death under tragic circumstances in the hunting field. The horse she was riding reared, and falling upon the lady inflicted such terrible injuries that she died shortly after being removed to an adjacent farm house. It was alleged by the plaintiff that Mottram, who was in at- tendance on Mrs. Cooper, abstracted her' purse while she was insensible and took out the gold, which Mr. Cooper now valued at £l. After Mrs. Cooper's death Mottram also I claimed the mare which caused, the accident. Mr. Cooper swore Mrs. Cooper had an independent estate, but that he supplied her with money to purchase the mare, which was kept for Mrs. Cooper's amusement, she being an excellent horsewoman.—The defence was that Mrs. Cooper and Mot- tram were partners respecting the purchase of hunting and other horses, but that in regard to this mare Mrs. Cooper I • origtnally bought her, and Mottram afterwards re-purchased because she proved restive in harness.—Judgment was re- served.

The s,-irmons were preached by the vicar, the Rev. G. Wyatt Ninis, and the Rev. Canon Biackburne, rector of Warming- ham awl rural deco of Cougleton and hon. canon of Chester Cathedral. The church has subsided most at the north- e.lFt corner, and there the Men succeeded in raising it about oight inches. This is the third time the church has had to raisr-d owing to subsidences. THE STATE OF DIE CROPS.
Below we give a continuation of cur reports on the state of the crops in this district. for which we are indebted to agricultural correspondents in the several localities named :

ACTON GRANGE.—Rye grass and clover will, it is thought, without exception, prove to be the lightest crop experienced for upwards of 20 years. Meadow hay is also light, except on low, damp parts. Eirly potatoes promise middling, providing we get rainfalls at once ; if not there will be a very light crop. Beans are looking fair, but not many are grown in this neighbourhood. In most fields pastures are only sufficient for the present ; cannot say how long they will last unless rain comes soon. Oats are look- ing very well, but wheat is only very midding. It is too soon to form any reliable opinion respecting late potatoes, swedes, mangolds, cabbages, carrots, eic., but the swedes are braiding fairly.

fledi.r:woori.—Corn as a rule is looking very poor, particu- larly spring sown wheat. Oats and barley are middling. Potatoes are fair; while the weather is against turnips, mangolds, and gras3, the latter being very bare in the bottom.

DARESBURY.—Wheat is late an] "thin of root." Oats generally are looking well. Grass crops are light ; and potatoes are late, and not as good as average. NEWTON-BY-DARESDDRY. The very wet autumn pre- vented wheat from being sown in proper time. Light soils will have the best of it with wheat this season. Spring-sown wheat on stiff, cold land, in many cases being a failure, has had to be made good by re-sowing with blazk oats, beans, or barley. I never remember so small an acreage of really good wheat. I know of fields that were intended for wheat, with four different crops growing in same field. Barley is little sown in this district, bat that sown where spring wheat failed is looking moderately well. Oats generally are look- ing well, but are beginning to suffer for want of rain, espe- cially those on the ley furrow. Beans are sown rather more than usual, and generally look promisigg. Potatoes in this district will be a fortnight later in the ifiarket than last veer, and the acreage of early kinds will be less, owing to the scarcity of seed. This crop is also in want of rain. Later kinds are looking well. The weather has been all that could be desired for working and clearing the ground for turnips. This has been done and the seed is sown, and is only waiting for a shower of rain, and they will be all a brood. The early crops of hay in most cases will be light; meadow and low damp pieces may do well. Public leys are barely stacked with cattle, owing to the scarcity of superfluous stock. Nothing shows plainer than this, that farmers are worse in the pocket than in previous seasons, and have no full over average crop to look forward to to fill up their purses. RIXTON-WITH-GLAZEBRCX)K.—Wheat will be under an average crop, oats are an average crop, a-id grass under an average crop. Root crops are looking very well. RAINFORD AND Dtsnucr.—Grass for hay, very light; oats, looking very well, a little burned by sun; barley, looking well; rye, only a moderate show; potatoes, coming very well ; mangolds coming up very well, but only a few are sown, as they have done badly other years ; turnips extremely well, not touched by the flies.

A correspondent in the Manchester Guardian writes:—l fear very much we are about to enter upon a season of light hay crcps. The cold winds which have prevailed for the last fortnialit or more and the want of rain combined have made havoc of the hay prospects, for grain appears to have stopped growing except the seed 'grass, which threatens to ripen before the undergrass is half ready for cutting. Another fortnight of such weather will leave us with little more than half a crop, if it reach so much as that. Almost everything is taking harm for want of rain except grain and potatoes that got a good start, but late sown grain looks anything but encouraging in many places. These remarks apply chiefly to South and South-West Lancashire and a portion of Cheshire which I have visited this week. Generally speaking, oats from Stretford to Heatley are looking well, but in some places the tips of the blades seem as if they had been bitten by the cold, and are quite brown. Potatoes are looking well, and cabbages also. Grasses are not so forward as they ought to be. About Lvmm I observed a field or two of artificial grasses which look pretty well, but they are late. Early potatoes and cabbages look strong and healthy, oats vary very much, and everything wants rain. There had been no rain beyond a very slight shower for eleven days, and farmers were complaining very much. From Speke forward to Liver- pool the want of rain was painfully felt. Oats are looking very badly and yellow in many places, and the yellow ket- lock has got the upper hand of the grain. Meadows are thin and light, and pastures are a ery bare; potatoes are in great need of moisture. It is sat prising how little pro• gress vegetation has made along here during the last few weeks. Upon the large marshes on each side of the Mersey there were numbers of young stock, and as far as one could see they were quite as well off for food as anywhere in the neighbourhood. Approaching the low flit tract of land which the Alt drains on the Aintree side, there is some good ryegrass and clover, and some good grain and potatoes, with here and there a field too vello with the ketlock. On the north side of that stream, how- ever, artificial grasses are exceedingly thin and without any bettoin grass. There is a very large area of potatoes, wLich is suffering for want of moisture. From. Maghull to Town Green matters are rather worse than nearer the Alt, and the prospects for the hay crop are anything but en- couraging. At Ormskirk there are complaints about the want of rain, and further northward the pastures are as bare as ever I saw them at any time of the year, affording the ineaaerest nibble for cattle. There is little to be net with that is satisfactory except the early sown crops ; the artificial grasses are very disappointing. Taming, tavartrs South- port from Burscough, some of the later oats looks ill, and here and there the ravages of the grub add to the ill effects of the unfavourab!e weather. Potatoes of which there is a large area planted, do .not wear that appearance of health that could be desired, nor are they so forward. The earliest planted here as elsewhere preseniNhe best appearance. On the moss matters are a little batter, bat rain is needed. All along the coast from Ainschile to Waterloo the crops were better than I expected to see them, though they want rain. Some of the pastures which are wholly on the sand are qu'te brown owing to the drought. From Olive Mount to Huy-ton and Rain hill grain is a good colour, and here and there is some very fair artificial grass, hut it is not growing much ; about the latter place grass is very light. On the , thin-soiled wet meadows about the Glaze there are many acres of very thin grass. It is not until one reaches the cultivated parts of Chat Moss that-traces of the rain which fell last Friday became evident. During the day I met with only one instance of haymaking, and that was a very light crop of rye grass. Beans generally are looking well, and are now in bloom. In several instances I met with a good show of turnips. L rte planted potatoes have not appeared so evenly an the early planted ones, and gaps'in the drills are visible. There is comparatively little grazing on the ground which I traversed. but what cattle I raw were look- ing well.

• Cetrnox TO BICYCLE Ittimis.—At the Newton Petty Sessions, on t-aturday, James Brown and Alfred Green were summoned for riding a bicycle without having a: proper lamp affixed.—The defendants did not appear.—P.C. Jones deposed that at twenty minutes to ten on the night of the 24th ultimo he saw the defendants ridirrg on their bicycles in Southworth-road, Newton. They were both without lamps, and he told them they would be reported.—The de- fendants were fined ss. and costs each.

COLLIERs' MEETING AT EARLESTOWN.—During the past few weeks the miners of this district have been holding a series of meetings with the view of rendering assistanCe to ite men of' North Staffordehirejwini are at:, present out on strike aghinst a 'proposed yeduction of 10 pen cent in their' Wages. Several' meetings have been beld at Heidock, Gelberns, &c, and on Thursday evening a number of ,the men assembled on the Earlestown maiket ground—where it it bad been announced a meeting would be held. There were not many colliers present. The principal speaker was Mr. John Cross, of St. Helens, who referred at eome length to the dispute in North Staffordshire, and maintained thlt the men of this and other parts of the country should band themselves together to support their fellow-workmen elsewhere in'thoir disputes and struggles. He hoped the men of.South-West Lancashire would render what assistance they needed, and unite to stem the evil which, if successful in North Staf- fordshire, would spread over the country. At the close of tie meeting a resolution was carried pledging the meeting to support the men of North Staffordshire to the utmost of their abilitv

ITHE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL. -- Before the Canal Committee, on Monday, Captain Graham Hills, marine surveyor to the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board, was examined at great length in opposition to the 84 heme. He gave statistics as to the condition of the tide- way., iznd the influence likely to be exerted by the proposed worts in ;t3.llPper portion. In his opinion the formation of training waltz would lead to a silting up of sand above Garstorrf with Consequent damage to the fairway. The Mersey, under present conditions, had the capacity of pre- serving a navigable channel through the bar, but he feared if the estuary was remodelled that deposits would continue unchecked. It was extremely probable that the upper estuary would gradually fill up and become first marsh and then land fit for cultivation. The witness, cross-examined for the promoters, agreed that similar works had proved most saccessful in the Seine, Tyne, Clyde, and other rivers, but dcubted their application in the Mersey, which had peculiarities of its own.

Mr. G. F. Lyster, principal engineer to the Mersey Docks Estate, was the only witness examined on Tuesday before the Ship Canal Committee in behalf of the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board, as petitioners against the Bill. He de- scribed the extent and capacity of the docks, basins, and quays on both sides of the river, which were managed by the Board. The tendency of the proposed works, he thought, would be to form banks of sand in front of the Liverpool dock entrances, and so interfere very seriously with traffic. In Mr. Lyster's judgment, the estimates of cost given by the promoters were egregiously inadequate, and, instead of three years being occupied in making the low-water channel, he considered the time would be much nearer ten years. The Chairman, before rising, intimated that the committee, in order to shorten the inquiry, would be prepared to sit for a longer period each day. In the Committee, on Wednesday; Mr. Lyster was cross- examined in regard to his estimates of the cost of making the proposed low-water channel. Mr. F. Vernon Harcourt, C E., author of several books on tidal streams and estuaries, gave evidence for the opponents in regard to the effect upon the Mersey channel of the proposed works: Before the Committee, on Thursday, Sir F. Bramwell was examined for the opponents, and predicted that the new channel would prove disastrous to the trade of Liverpool and Birkenhead by forming banks of sand in the Mersey and obstructing navigation. Other engineers having given similarly hostile testimony, Captain Kennedy, of the Inman line, smoke as to probable effects of the intended works from a seaman's point of view. He thought it would be impos- sible for large ships to get out and over the bar in one tide. It would be dangerous to navigate the low-water channel at night, and quite impossible in thick weather. Mr. Hornby, chid, man of the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board, was under examination when the Committee adjourned.

The Morning Post states, with regard to the Manchester Ship Canal Bill, that" the committee will probably, report in favour of the Bill, subject, however, to certain stringent financial restrictions."

div.head: RATING OF NEWTON LAKE.
div.p: THE RATING OF NEWTON LAKE.
LANE AGAIN BEFORE THE COURT.

At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Satay day, before Geo. McCotquodale, R. Houghton, and C. Pilkington, Esqs., John Lane was summoned to show cause why a distress warrant should not be issued against him for the payment of a rate. Mr. Houghton (the assistant overseer) stated that the case had been adjourned until that day for the purpose of allow- ing the defendant to appeal at the Quarter Sessions. The defendant was assessed for the poor rate in the amount of 13s. 4d. in respect of landing stage on Newton mere. He had demanded the rate, and"the defendant had not paid it. —The defendant said be would ask Mr. Houghton what he was really rated for. On the first occasion- he was rated for the landingstage alone, but there was no landing stage; on the secend itwas for the landing stage and Newton mere, and now it was landing stage on Newton mere. The case I had been taken before the Assessment Committee at War- rington, and he appeared to refute the false statements made at that court. —The Chairman: This is a court of justice, and no man has a right to say that another has made a false statement—The defendant: I can prove It.—The Chair- man: Will you listen to me? No man has a right to say that another has made a false statement. —The defendant: Not if he can prove it P—The Chairman: You have no right to make it.—The defendant quoted from a report of a meeting of the Assessment Committee, and maintained that be could not be rated as he was neither owner or occupier. There bad been no landing stage since 1881, when it was pulled up. There was nothing to rate.—The Deputy Clerk (Mr. White): Can you prove that there has been no land- ing stage since 1881 '1 —The defendant: I can sir, and I will call a witness to prove it.—A virtness named Hall then de- posed that he remembered the landing stage on Newton mere being taken up In the early part of October, 1881.— The defendant: I heard they were going to lay a rate, and I took up the landing stage. It was only a few old planks worth about ss.—Mr: White: Mr. Houghton, do you say I that Mr. Lane has occupation ef that lake so as to have con- trol over it P—The defendant: Control over it! I cannot let a man go and fish there. Mr. White Is he occupier, Mr. Houghton P—The defendant: Is be occupier? No.—Mr. Houghton stated that as far as occu- pation of the lake was concerned the defendant had receipts • from the lake, and had a benefit from it—The Chairman asked if he could give leave to fish in it ?—The defendant: No, sir.—Mr. Houghton: I don't know, sir.—The rate , book was then produced, and Mr. Houghton stated that the ' gross estimated rental of the place was £23 10s., and the rateable value £2o.—The- defendant, John Lane, was then sworn.—The Deputy Clerk: What is your position ?—The defendant said he was a servant under William John Legh, Esq., and his terms were 10s. per week. The rest of his wages he bad to make up by letting the boats on the water. His duties were to look after poaching and illegal fishing. There were several occupiers of Newton lake.—The Chair- man : We have heard the case, and had the advise of our law clerk, and the case is dismissed.
ROBBERY FROM THE NEWTON STATION BOOK-STALL.

Before George McCorquodale, R. Houghton', and C. Pilk- ington, Esqrs., at the Newton Town Hall, on Saturday last, John Johnson, John Lynch, and Peter Redmond, of Earles- town, were again charged, on remand, with stealing several packs of cards and two books, together of the value of 10s, from Messrs. W. H. Smith and Son's book-stall at Newton Bridge Station, on the 27th ult. Johnsen pleaded guilty, and Mr. H. L. Riley, cf St. Helens, appeared for Lynch and Redmond, both of whom pleaded not guilty.—Mr. Preston, of Liverpool, solicitor to the London and North-Western Railway Company, prosecuted, and stated that the case ap- peared to he very clear against the prisoners, and that the robbery had been a very bare-faced one.—George Watkins, a lad, living at Warrington, and employed by Messrs. W. H. Smith and Son deposed that about five o'clock on the Saturday afternoon in question, he locked up the bookstall at Newton Bridge Station. Everything was then safe.—Charles Watkins, tit-other of the last witness, also employed by the sane firm, stated that about eight o'clock on the following Monday morning he opened the bookstall at Newton Station. He afterwards missed several packs of cards and two books, one of which was entitled "Who breaks pays." He did not know the name of the other hook.—Peter Wilson, a bottlemaker, residing in Houghton- street, Earleatown, stated that about a quarter past three o'clock en the Sunday morning he and some of his " mates " went to Newton Station for the purpose of meeting a friend from Scotland. He saw the prisoners on the platform, near to the bookstall. Johnson opened the bookstall and commenced to read a book. Witness told him to put the book back and not get other people into trouble. alley afterwards left the station.—John Mulhern, Gas-street, BArlestown, de- posed that he bought a new pack of cards from Johnson for Oct. Johnson told him he hid purchased it for 90.—James Louis Oulton, of Earlestown, stated that he SAW i.ynch with a new pack of cards in his possession. He said he had got them in a railway train.—P.C. Spencer, of Newton, stated that from information he received he went to Johnson's house and examined if. He found a new pack of cards therein and took Johnson into cusody. He afterwards ap- prwhended Lynch and Redmond. On being charged John- son said "I, John Lynch, and Peter Redmond were on the platform at Newton Bridge railway station on Sunday morn- ing last. I saw a piece of string under the book- stall door and I pulled the string. The door flew open and I took a pack of cards. Lynch and Redmond took a pack of cards each, and Lynch took a book—the name of the book was •‘ Who breaks pays.'" The prisoner Redmond replied "I never saw the string." and Lynch said "I never saw the string nor any- thing of the bookstall. I never took the cards nor anything else. We came from Warrington together by the train arriving at Warrington at three o'clock, and arrived at New- ton Bridge at a quarter past three on Sund iy morning."— Mr. Riley maintained that what one prisoner said was only evidence against himself, and that the case againet his clients must be considered as if the prisoner Johneon had never said a word. He submitted there was not a tittle of evi- dence against either Lynch or Redmond, and that there was nothing to show that they had stolen either cards or books. , —He proceeded to call a number of witnesses who stated ' that the prisoners Lynch and Redmond left the station to- Athol. leaving Johnson near the bookstall.—The Bench dis- charged Lynch and Redmond, and Johnson, who said be was drunk at the time and did not know what he was doing, was fined 20s and casts, or, in default of payment, one month's imprisonment.

TktS LAabuu MARKET.—The labur market;remaihe un- sett'. d, although there is plenty of work'to be had in many distalets. Building operations and railway and public works construction are in full swing, and several large con- tracts have just been decided, and men wanted. The iron trade is spmewhat quiet, some works being only partially going. In colliery districts half-time only is in some cases being made, and in North Staffordshire the ttike is now in its fifth week,'hut perhaps it may be approaching au end, as about 600 men resumed work last Monday. Engineering and shipbuilding dre very brisk, and likely to be so for some time to come. At Birmingham most trades are fairly busy; and at Sheffield, with the elception of the file trade, owing to the continued strike, all, branches of trade are busy. —The Labour News.

div.head: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.

The Monthly meeting was held at the Board-room, Alforde chambers on Tuesday afternoon. Mr. F. H. Gossage pre- sided, and there were also present Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. R. Carey, T. Handley, F. U. Pankhurst, Dr. Forster, .1. Mid- wood, B. Dutton, E. Medley, S. Sadler, R. Webster, J. R. Johnson, S. Houeaton, J. T. Allen (clerk), Hinginson (sur- veyor), Dickson .(nuisance inspector.) THE LATE LAW CLITEM. The following letter, dated the 25th Maw, received from the Local Government Board, was read :—" I am directed by the Local Government Board to acknowledge the receipt of your letters of the 4th, 18th, and 19th inst., with reference to the costs incurred by- the Widnes Local Board in opposing the London and North-Western (additional powers) Bill, 1831. ith respect to the explanation of Mr. Beasley, a copy of which accompanied your letter of the 4th inst., relating to the application of the Local Board for the Board's approval under the Municipal Corporations (borough Runde) Act, 1872, I am directed to state that Mr. Beasley is apparently under a misapprehensiox in thinking that he wrote to the Board, in reply to their letter of the 29th October, 1881, explaining that the advertisement of the notice of the meeting of the Local Board was published 10 clear days prior to the meeting being held. No such letter was received by the Board, nor was any further application made on behalf of the Local Board for the Board's approval of the resolution of the Local Board to oppose the Bill. The Board feel 'much doubt whether, after so long an interval, they could properly give their approval to the resolution, but they are prepared to consider any representations which the Local Board may wish to make on this point. The Board desire at the same time to be furnished with a state- ment of the amount of costs and expenses in relation to the opposition to the Bill, which are now outstanding, and of persons to whom they are owing."—The letter was re- ferred to committee.
' UUTCHINSON'S TRUSTEES AND TILE SEWERS.

The Cr.unn read the following -letter which he had re- °died Warrington, 4th June, 1883. Dear Sir, Butchiamn's Trustees and Arbitration,—ln accordance with the promise made at the hearing on Saturday we send you herewith form of resolution to be passed by your Board if they approve of it, as was done by all the members present at the hearing.—Yours truly, ROBERT DAVIES & Co."—Form of resolution : —" The arbitrators and umpire having at the reference now pending between the Local Board and Mr. Hutchinson's trustees unanimously re- commended that the Widnes Local Board should eutiertake to make good any damage now done or hereafter to be done to the sewers of Mr. Hntchinson's trustees daring the construction of their own sewerage works to the satis- faction of the umpire, so as to save an award for a fixed arbitrary and necessary speculative sum upon this account, resolved that the Local Board do accept such recommenda- tion, and do hereby agree to carry out the same."—Mr. T. HANDLEY said he was present at the meeting where that resolutibn was suggested. It was stated that Hutchinson's trustees had claimed £6OO for damages done to their sewer, and the arbitrators and the umpire thought it best for the Board to pass that resolution, and save the umpire from giv- ing an award for damages.—The CLUBMAN remarked that it would be perfectly safe for the Board to pass that resolu- tion without going any further.—Mr. CAREY moved, and Mr. HANDLEY seconded the resolution, which was carried.— Messrs. Johnson, Sadler, and Webster did not vote. MOSS BROOK 'RIDGE. A letter dated the 12th inst. had been received from Mr. Henry Mather enclosing an account for £lOl 10s. in the snit Teebay v. Widnes Local Board with regard to Moss crook Bridge. Mr. Mather had also forwarded a second Setter, in which was enclosed a bill for extras amounting to £127 12s. 6d., and asking for immediate payment —ln silswer to the chairman, Mr. MIDWOOD said he could not tell anything about the extras, but he had better make a state- ment as to the damage-, as he was appointed by the Board to watch the case at London on behalf of the Highway Com- mittee. The judge's decision was that in case Mr. Mather could substantiate his claim to damages, he (the judge) would graat an inquiry in the matter; so that he (Mr. Mid- wood) did not see that the Board were responsible in any way to Mr. Mather. It was for the surveyor to certify whether Mr. Mather was entitled to the extras.—The letter wail referred to the Highway Committee. PROPOSED NEW WORKS FOR WIDNES. Messrs. James H. Dennis and Co, of the Macclesfield Patent Sulphate of Copper Company, wrote to the clerk as fellows:—" Referring to your favour of the 7th mat, we Mad that we shall require 250,000 to 300 000 gallons of water per wech at our contemplated new works in your town. Would it not suit you better to make us a special quotation for the supply of your water rather than to put us to the expense of sinking wells, whereby you would lose the chance of the business. Please let us know promptly what is lowest rate you can quote." GAS COMMITTEE.
The minutes of this committee stated that the water in stook en May 23rd, 1883, was 9,099,529 gallons. The illu- minating power of gas during the month had averaged 18.53 candles.

div.head: GAS AND WATER OFFICES.
div.p: GAS AND WATER OFFICES.

Mr. Richard White, Hale Bank, wrote asking on what terms he could have a supply of about 200 gallons of water weekly, to be carted from the yard or elsewhere. The clerk was instructed to reply the charge would be 6d per load.— The minutes wer passed on the motion of Mr. PANICHURST, seconded by Mr. FORSTIR.
HIGHwAY COMMITTEE: ROAD IMPROVEMENTS : MR. WEBSTER IN _PURSUIT OF INFORMATION.

Oa the 21st nit. the Highway Committee inspected the sewer for the stoppage of which Messrs. W. H. Kershaw and Co. had made a claim. The clerk was instructed to inform the claimants that the committee did not consider them- selves liab:e, on ae:: far an npportunity of inspecting the sewer when opened out for cleaning. At a subsequent sneeting, the clerk was instructed to urge the railway com- pany to proceed at once with the work connected with the I bridges at Lugsdaie, Appleton, and Farnworth. A letter was read from the Widnes Alkali Company re the evidence given by Mr. Worthington about the delay at Ann-street level crossing. The committee deferred consideratioc of the letter pending the reply from the railway company. It was re- commended that the Ferry approach be altered as per plan, at an estimated cost of £250; that the parapet in Mersey-road between Church and Oakland streets be flagged ; that the stone pavement near to Waterloo-road level crossing be taken up and relaid with macadam ; and that a set crossing be put 1n at the junction of 011ier-street with Victoria-road. The surveyor was instructed to ask Messrs. Knowles and Dutton it they would give a little land to widen Lugsdale-road. The plan of 135 houses at Mill Brow for Messrs. W. H. Kereh iw and Co. were submitted, and the surveyor was in- structed to examine and report.—lr. MIDWOOD moved the confirmation of the, minutes, and remarked that the com- mittee wished the Board to go into committee to consider Messrs. Kershaw's case. The question of improving the Perry approach bad been before the committee several times and it was now proposed to carry Mersey-road through to :the water's edge. The delay had arisen because the com- mittee had been endeavouriog to obtain a portion of the money required for the work from the L. and N.-W. Railway Company,but they had been unable to do so. Messrs. Greenall and Co. had offered to give the Board VIO towards the cast, and the Board had with that sum a balance in hand sufficient to meet the expenditure. They had also had the Land given them. It was, he thought, therefore only reason- able that the Board should carry out this extension for the benefit of the ratepayers. The committee's estimate for the year's expenditure—£3,s6B—was £B9 higher than last year. This was explained by the fact that the committee had to provide £235 worth of metal more than they had last year, because the roads were not up to the mark; and they de- sired to keep them in thorough order. But for this item the estimate would have been £145 lower than last year. The roacedarnising of Waterloo-road level crossing would be a great improvement.—The motion was seconded. Mr. Weneerset said be saw the committee recommended that re- pairs be done to the Appleton property, and he should like to know from Mr. Midwood what per centage that property Was flinging in, why it was built, why it was bought, and for what purpose? Mr. Midwood seemed to be getting into the spending department since he was promoted chair- man of the committee, and recommended the expenditure of £250 on the Ferry approach. He should like to know more about it before he gave his vote. Mr. HANDLEY, in movisg the adoption of the Finance Committee's minutes, said it was usual at this time of the year for the chairman of the Finance Committee to lay before the members an account of the expenditure for the past year, and he thought be should be able to lay an account before them which would be satisfactory to all. The estimate for the year ending the 31st Marc', 1883, was £8,686 14s 2d, and the amount really expended was £7,705 17s. The estimates of the different committees were—Hospital £255 10s, expended £203 lOs 2d, surplus £5l 19s 10d; Health £1,107, expended £835, surplus £272; Highway £3,478 12s, ex- pended £3,305 2s 7d, surplus £173 98 sdl Finance £3.855 19s Bd, expended £3,362 4s 3d, surplus £493 15s sd; market estimated to realise a credit balance of £lO is 6d, produced £5B 53 Bil, surplus £45 183 21; showing on the whole year a surplus of £1,037 2s 101 The rate was estimated to pro- duce £8,400 up to March 31st. It produced, however, £8,700 6s 101, but at the date named there was owing £139 8s 81, most of which had since come in, so that the rate had produced £439 15s 61 more than was estimated, bring- ing the total surplus to £1,46 183 4d. The profits on the gas works for the past year amounted to £2,811 163 51, but a loss of £B2O 15s lid nn the waterworks reduced the profits to £1 991 18s 101, which, added to the surplus from the rate, made a total surplus of £3,467 18s 101. This was a state of affairs which he was sure must be very satisfactory to the members of the Board. The next question was what should be done with this surplus. It would be in the recol- lection of the Board that some years ago £17,400 was bor- rowed to be expended on public roads. That sum was spent, but the total amount debited against the public roads was £15,547 15s 21, leaving £1,852 4s 10d to be made up. The Finance Committee proposed that that sum should be take. from the surplus to make the account square. The rest of the surplus would go te pay off bad balances owing at the bank. At the present time thilinances of the Board were In a very healkiLy aoiid!ti37,l; ttG 133ard wag ifioß clear of all debt. ([Lear, hear.) Toe estimates for the year ending March 25th, 1884, were :—Highway Committee, £3,568; Health, £892; Hospital, £233 103; Finance, £4,304; total, £8,997 101. But from this was to be deducted an expected credit balance of £56 103 from the market, which would make the total estimate £8,941. These estimates were for twelve menthe. He should explain to the Board that in February a resolution was passed that in future the rate should be laid every nine months. When that resolution was passed it was thought that they would be able to lay a rate in April or May, but circumstances had interfered with that arrangement. The clerk and the surveyor had been in London, and had been unable to get the rate out, and it would now be July or August before they could do so. The Finance Committee though, it would be foolish to lay a rate for nine months, be- cause as it would be up on the 31st December they would have little time to get it in. It would, besides. be more economical and more convenient to lay rate for 12 months. (Hear, hear.) A rate for nine months would have to be is 8d in the £, which would be Id less than last year, but a 12 months' rate would be 41 less than the previous year, which must be particularly satisfactory to the ratepayers. List year the assessment for the township was£lo6,l4o, and a2s 4d rate nroduced £8.900. The assessment had been raised to £123,767, and a 2s rate on the same basis as last year would bring in as much money, viz., £8,895. The ' committee therefore recommended tbat the resolution refer- ring to the nine menthe' rate be rescinded, and that a rate of 2s in the for 1% months be laid.—Dr. O'KEEFFE seconded the motion.—Mr. WznsrEn said Mr. Handley had spoken in glowiug terms, but he should like to ask him whether the Board had done all the work that the money was estimated for, or whether they had paid off the old debts of the Board, and if so to what amount ?—Nlr. POLICE INSPECTION AT Sr. HELENS.—At noon, on Turz- day, Captain Alison, Deputy Chief Constable of the county, visited at. Helens and made an inspection of the clothing and appointments of the men who are stationed in that division, and also made an examination of the police build- ings. There were on parade Supt. Johnson, six sergeants, and forty-three constables, the remainder being on, duty. The men presented a smart appearance, all of them wearing the new uniform which has just been supplied. The cells and offices were also inspected, and the books scrutinised. Everything appeared to be in a satisfactory condition.

-- • - The Lancet is glad to be able to state that beyond hie grey hairs, Mr. Bright showed hardly any traces of time-wrought changes at the mass meeting at Birmingham on Wednesday. For nearly an hour his voice held out clear and strong, and only after he had been successfully cilling upon it to carry his words to over 20,000 persons for that time did he get hoarse. To those who recall how Mr. Bright has twic3 been laid aside from all work for considerable periods by serious ill- ness it will be particularly gratifying that ke is enjoying such a hale old age.

Mr. Peter Taylor is beginning to have some hope for his anti-vaccination resolution, which he has put down for Tues- day, June JP. He will ask the House to declare its opinion that "it is inexpedient and unjust to enforce vaccination under penalties upon those who regard it as unadvisable and dangerous." Had Mr. Hopwood moved that resolution a few weeks ago, as he intended to do, it would have met easily with its coup de grace ; but the accident to Dr. Corry has made many members uneasy. The fact that vaccina- tion has turnect a very clever man into something like a lunatic, though his mental weakness is only temporary, has made a profound impression.

The rumour that the Government on Thursday decided upon an autumn session is absolutely untrue. The Govern- ment is not prep red for an autumn session. On the contrary, it is strongly opposer to it. But it is very likely to take all Tuesdays henceforth for Government business, and to retain Friday morning sittings. Saturday sittings are also expected early next month.

At the present rate of progress about six months would' be needed to pass the Criminal Code Bill through the Grand Committee on Law. The first line of clause 12 has been under consideration for two days and a half, and is not yet done with. The Irish members are the oause of the delay. At Thursday's sitting Mr. Parnell spoke six times, Mr. Marum six, Dr. Commins three, and Mr. Sexton, Colonel Nolan, and M. P. Martin twice each, their remarks in almost every case being lengthy. Never- theless there was practically only one question to be settled—namely, whether the power of holding an inquiry without a charge being made against any particular per- son should be entrusted to the paid or unpaid magistracy. Two amendments were disposed of in the course of the sitting, but 61 still stand against the clause.

Christie's Rows, in King-street, were crowded an Thurs- day by persons anxious to see the famous Limoges enamels, brought hither from Blenheim Palace for sale. It is the best colleection of the kind in the country—not very large, as far as numbers go, but, as the prices given indicate, ex- ceedingly choice. In addition to the enamels there was offered a table of rare beauty, inlaid with Sevres plaques of special size and design. It is said, and doubtless with more correctness than attends many similar statements, that this table was once toe property of Marie Antoinette. A little less than ten years ago the Duke of Marlborough lent these heirloom to the South Kensington Museum, where they attracted much attention. Now they come to the hammer, and the ducal purse will be temporarily replenished by the sale of treasures for which, as Mr. Chamberlain would say, the present duke toiled not, neither did be spin. What with an earl in the county court and a duke looting his family palace, the aristocracy seem in a bad way.
COAL DEALER FINED FOR SELLING

It is no wonder that Mr. Chamberlain's out-spoken speech at Birmingham has excited a good deal of attention. Mr. Chamberlain is not accustomed, in g-neral conversation, to conceal his views on some big political questions near at band; bnt it is startling to some and encouraging to others to find him thus boldly grappling with these ticklish ques- tions in a speech delivered in an exceedingly public place. Mr. Warton, with something more than his average astute- ness, has seen the opportunity of at least endeavouring to draw from the Premier an avowal which may be damaging one way or another, either as associating the Government with Mr. Chamberlain's views, and so giving a flip to Tory opposition, or inducing him, in whatever guarded language, to repudiate them. He intends to ask whether the Premier has read the speech, and whether the views expressed are those of her Majesty's Government. 1

Surprise has been expressed at the great difference there is between the estimates of the rival engineers of the cost of executing the proposed ship canal works in the estuary of the Mersey. It should be borne in mind that this difference is easily explained. The engineers 3f the dock board esti- mate the cost of dredging rock at 6s 81 per cubic yard, whereas Mr. Leader Williams and other engineers put down the figure at 2s 6d. It is somewhat remarkable that the engineers who fix the price at 6s 8d have never carried out any dredging works, while all the enaineers called by the promoters have been actively engaged in this occupation, and should therefore have a more intimate knowledge of the subject than their other professional brethren have. In the Clyde. the Tees, and the Tyne, the actual cost was from 5d to 7d per yard, and I understand that one of the largest dredg- ing contractors of the kingdom is prepared to come before the committee and state that he would be willing to do the work for 9d per yard. Between 6s B'l and 9d there is a great difference, and this fact must to a large extent detract from the reliableness of Mr. Lyster's estimate.

Mr. Labouchere is by no moans disheartened by Mr Bishop's great success on Tuesday night, when he named the figures on the hidden bank note. Since Mr. Bishop de- clines to work with Mr. Firth, Mr. Labouchere has to-day written a letter renewing his challenge, whilst placing the conditions on a much wider basis. He now offers the choice of fifty members of Parliament, with any one of whom he will lodge a thousand pound note, which note eliall be Mr. Bishop's if he guesses the number. Should he fail with one member, he may make his second guess with another. With his peculiar humour he has selected his fifty members largely from the Treasury bench and the front Opposition bench, such respectable names as those of E)ir Stafford Sorthcote and the Home Secretary appearing on the list. But he does not confine his selection to the front benches. Ile takes representative men like Mr. Parnell, Lord Ran- dolph Churchill, and even Lord Mayor Dawson. This seems a fair challenge, and it will be interesting to see what recep- tion it meets with.

Lord George Hamilton is sorry he spoke about Mr. God- ley's proximate appointment to the office of Permanent 17nder-Secretary for India. It baying been made Wear that the report of this appointment, circulated a week ago, is well founded, Lord George Hamilton, on Thursday, amid the cheers from the Conservatives, gave notice to ask what age Mr. Godley has reached, and whether it is hot a fact that in his new office he will have 600 clerks under him, some of whom have served thirty or forty years. This is a novel way of challenging an appointment, but of all men one of the young sons of the Duke of Abercorn was the worst per- son in the world to ask it. Colonel Nolan, jumping up in his hot way, gave notice that when the questknis put he will ask what ago Lord George Hamilton was when, by the favour of Mr. Disraeli, he was appointed to the still higher post of Under-Secretary for India, and whether Ire had not under him upwards of 600 subordinates, many. of 'whom had nerved many years. A roar of laughter from both sides of the House greeted this happy hit. Lord George did not laugh, but sat diligently following his favourite occupa- tion of tearing up bits of paper. It is probable he will not put the question which has such an unfortunate rider.

Dean Swift was once walking down Whitehall when a man jumped from a top storey window, and, falling on the ground below, killed himself. While the crowd was gather- ing round the spot an elderly gentleman came up, and in- quired in a business-like air, "Well, who is she ? " The Dean said, "It isn't a woman, it's a man." "Oh, I see that perfectly well," rejoined his questioner, "but what woman has been the cause of it all ? " This appears to be the case with France. The Empress Eugenie regards- the Franco- German war as her special feat, the annexatian of Tunis is said to be the handiwork of a daughter of, Eve, and now, certain of the French journals are discovering that the female element is preponderating in the Tonqnin business, and they bitterly inveigh against this expensive policy of "All for her."

The financial affairs of "an illustrious person," to use Thackeray's phrase, are now engaging the attention of soc:ety. The person in question, is closely connected with the Royal Familyond the report is that ha has come under obligations which he is not able to discharge. It is probable that some sort of settlement will be arrived at with his creditors. In the meantime, faowing the example of bumbler people,,he is going to live-abroad, for some time ir, order to economise.

div.head: SHOCKING DISCLOSURES,
div.p: SHOCKING DISCLOSURES,

At Warrington Borough Police Court, on Tuesday, Wit- Item Clark, a fairly dressed labeuring man, and Esther Clark, his wife, of dissipated appearance, residing at 47, Old Road, Latchford, were charged on warrant, before Major Cartwright and Alderman Chandley, with, being the parents of a female child named Susannah Clark, aged 15 months, having unlawfully and wilfully neglected to provide ade- quate food and clothing for such child (they having means and ability to do so), whereby the health of the child was eer;ottely injured. Mr. J. C. Sutton, clerk of the Warrington Union, prosecuted on behalf of the Board of Guardians. The prisoners pleaded not guilty.—Mr. T. J. Garnett, re- lieving officer of No. 3 district of the Warriugton Union, said from information he received from the police he went to No. 47, Old Road, Latchford, where the prisoners live, on Monday, at two o'clock. The male prisoner was working for Mr. Riley. at the Rope and Anchor, and as far as he knew he was in constant work. He found at the house the female prisoner, who was considerably the worse for drink. There was also a little child, about three years of age, beside the table, and near to her another child on some straw in a cradle. The child was lying in the cradle in an almost naked 'condition. and was kicking its legs about. He went for the medical officer for the Union, who visited the house with him. When they went into the house at half-past three the same afternoon there was no one downstairs. The door was closed, and they got a neighbour to open it. On pro- ceeding upstairs he found the female prisoner in bed with the two youngest children. She was asleep, and by calling out they awoke her, and she sat up in bed. She was then stupitied, he considered, through drink. Dr. Spinks ex- amined the child, and he (witness) took out warrants for the apprehension of the prisoners. He did not see anything of the man dating his visits to the house, and the wife told him all her children were like this one when teething. The child was between 15 and 16 months old.—Major Cart- wright: When was your attention drawn to the child? I received a note late on Sunday night from the police. The prisoners have never received any relief from me.— Asked if he had anything to ask the wit- ness, the male prisoner said what the witness said was quite right; he would vouch for it.— Jane Longworth, a married woman, residing in School-street, near the prisoners', eaid she had known the baby ever since it was born, which was shortly after she went to live in School-street. It would be 16 months old on the 25th inst. She had found it r.ecessary during the time she Mad lived in the street frequently to go into the house and feed the child, as there was no one in and it was crying. She had known it left in the house from dinner time. The husband had come home to his dinner, but there had been none ready for him, and he had gone back to his work; and she had gone into the house in the middle of the afternoon, when there had been no one in but a boy on the cradle rocking it, and had fed the baby with the bottle. Mr. Sutton : For how much of the day has the wife been away when this hap- pened? Well, sir, perhaps all day. From morning until night? Yes, when she has known her hus- band has not been coming home.—And the cries of the child attracted your attention? Yes, sir.-9n Sunday afternoon the husband ran his wife out of the house, and Mrs. Ellison went in and lifted the baby up. Witness had a drop of milk and a bun which she broke up and gave to the child. Mrs. Ellison said they would wash the child, and they took it into witness's house for that purpose, but the cloth they dried it with they had to put in the fire as the child was covered with vermin. The baby ate the bun and milk ravenously as though it was in a state of great hunger.— What condition was she in then? She was drunk. The father was crying, and I said "do you want any dinner," and he said " No he had had enough dinner when he came in and saw the child like that." Zie said he could feed those children who wanted a" betty," but the baby he could not feed. The mother always said when witness went in that her child was as good as her's (witness's), and it was healthy.—By Major Cartwright: The mother had since blamed her for going into the house, and said she had no business there.—Miss E. Winstanley said she had frequently seen the child since its birth. Until some time after it was an ordinary child. She had noticed'the child falling off. She had known it left in the house alone on some dirty straw, almost naked—with just a little scarf round it. She had taken it food for two or three months. She first went in when it was about ten months old.—P.S. Bowen deposed to apprehending the pri- soners under warrant. The woman was drunk, and she was also drunk when he Saw her first. On Sunday after- noon, about 20 minutes past three, he saw a largo crowd round the door of the house, and he went there. He saw the female prisoner dirty and drunk, and on account of the many harvestmen about he asked the husband to let her in. He did so, and witness saw the child lathe cradle. The house was in a filthy condition, and he at once reported the circumstances to the Chief-Censtable, who directed him to see Mr. Harbourne. He saw Mr. Harbourne, who directed him to see Mr. Garnett. He did not see anything in the house but a chaff bed, very dirty, and a dry 41b. loaf. When he apprehended the male prisoner at his work he had 7s. 6d. in his possession. He had been constantly in work for the last 13 years to his (witness's) knewledge.—Pri- .er ! And von never saw me out of order in any way.— Witness said there were five children altogether. The woman belonged to those Bates's, the pigeon flyers, and the grand- mother's house, where the children slept on Monday night, was almost as filthy as the prisoners'.—Dr. Spinks said Mr. Garnett went for him on Monday afternoon about three o'clock to go to the prisoners' house. The door was fastened inside, and he looked through the window, but could see no- body inside. A neighbour opened the door for them, and he sent Mr. Garnett upstairs to see if the wife was there. When Mr. Garnett got up he saw her on the bed and celled wit- ness up. He went and saw her sitting up in the bed. He went round towards her but could only see one child, and she picked up the other from beside her. He then SAW it was a mere skeleton. He examined it and found it wae a healthy child but was simply suffering from the effects of starvation and want of food. He advised Mr. Garnett to ' obtain a warrant, and have Om woman locked up, and to send the child to the workhouse. Mr. Garnett did so, and Ithat morning he weighed and measured the child. He found it only weighed 7lh 13azs (which was the weight of a new- born ckild ; and was 24 inches long (2 inches longer than the average length of a new-born infant). It might have I been a very fine child if it had had the common necessaries of life.—Major Cartwright : Even now it is not diseased ? : Dr. Spinks: No. I may tell you when she picked it up it 'seized hold of the mother's breast and began to suck in a very ravenous manner, as if it wanted food very bay.— The male prisoner said he did all that lay in his power for ' his family. He worked hard daring the week, and when he went home he gave his wife his money as a man ought to do. Sometimes when he went home there was no one in the house but the children running about like rats, and when he found his wife she was rolling drunk. She was drank every day more or less. She pawned everything. He had as many pawn tickets as would cover the court table. He get £3 worth of goods only laet month to make them com- fortable, and by the end of the week after every one of them had gone. He had gone many and many a time with- out dinner in order to feed his children.—Major Cartwright said from his experience he could not hold the husband blameless. If he had had a spark of the man about him he would have left his wife and not allow the poor baby to starve in the manner it had. The wife was literally murdering it. A little more and they would have been brought up on a very different charge. There was no question something had been said in favour of the tnan—that lie. was a steady man and attended to his work. Through the influence of biz; brother. magistrate they had come to the conclusion to bind him. over to appear when c tiled upon. [The male prisoner e Thank you, sir. lam much obliged to you ] He felt very strongly era the sub- ject, and had he been left to hitneelf he should have com- mitted him to gaol, certainly. However, he must in future see the children were properly looked after and properly cared for. [The prisoner:. Thank you, sir. lam much obliged to you, sir.] As to Mrs. Clark,. he for one could' not but feel the utmost contempt for a wotnen who brought herself to her position, and he was exceedingly sorry the- magistrates had not po wen , o give her even inure punish- ment than they were going to do. For months she had, been torturing the infaot—in fact she had I.)en killing it by Inc 3, and in his opinion it only required a very little time Imager, and she would have been the death of it. lie never saw anything in such a state in his life, and therefore. the Bench gave her the utmost punishment they could, that w.ts that she he committed to the House of correction,.faar !six calendar months with hard labour. He hoped it would I' he a lesson to her and others who starved their children Alderman Chandiev thought the Bench would only be-doing , their duty in expressing their 3.4i,footiori at the part- P'.S. Bowen hod taken in this matter. 'lnformation oti4lit..aer- t ..inly to have been given hy tbe neighbours, and the i-mti.on P.S. Bower. had taken they thought was very much. 'D his credit.

div.head: SHORT WEIGHT.
div.p: SHORT WEIGHT.

At Warrington Borough Court, on Monday, Fre- derick Al'mark, coal dealer, Salford, and John Salt, coal dealer, 101, Winwick-street, Warrington, were summoned for having on the sth inn unlawfully sold to Elijah Place, a certain bag of coal, purporting to contain 1 cwt, and on being weighed was found 15Ib 10-lozs. short; and further, with selling a quantity of coal otherwise than by weight. —Mr. J. L. Whittle,deputy town clerk, appeared to prose- cute on behalf of the Corporatior ; and Mr. Percy Davies appeared for the defendants. Jr. Whittle, after stating the section of the Act under which the. case was brought, was about to make a statement, when Mr. P. Davies objected and said he bad no right, net being a solicitor, to make any statement of that kind. What was the good of passing an examination to be a lawyer if Mr. Whittle was allowed to do s, ?—Major Cartwright: I thought you were the deputy town clerk, Mr. Whittle.—The Deputy-Mayor: I think that has been satis- factorily settled some time ago.—Mr. Davies: I leave it to Mr. White to sty whether he has any right to say it.—The Clerk: I don't know what he is going to say.—Major Cart- wright: I think you are venturing an delicate ground.— The Deputy-Mayor: Let us get on with the evidence.—Mr. Elijah Place, market inspector, said on the day named the defendant Salt and three other men were going along Win- wick-street delivering coal. They delivered coal all the length of the street, and never weighed a single bag. He then went up Pinner's-brow, and down Oliver-street, and entered a shop. He gave the shopkeeper is to get a cwt. of coal, which was brought into the shop, and put in a corner. After the coal had been discharged, and the man had gone away, he had the coal gathered up and put in another sack which was taken to his office. The man had a suspicion something was wrong, as he came back and asked the shop- keeper to let him have the coal back. After this he (wit- ness) followed the men to Watkin-street and got their names. Salt said the coal belonged to Allmark, but after a time a man came to his office, and said the coal belonged to Salt. The name on the bury was Henry Allmark, and the man said Allmark had bought the ham and hired it to Salt.— Cross-examined: Although Salt had a machine on the lutry he did not use it.—The person who purchased the coal gave confirmatory evidence.—Mt. Davies said he had advised the defendant to plead guilty to selling the coal otherwise than by weight, as it was a trivial charge. It was the practice not to weigh the coal, as they were not bound to do so unless asked. Last Satur- day week the partnership existing between Allmark and Salt was dissolved, but the cart was let by Allmark to Salt at a week. He was instructed that every one of the bags on the cart was weighed out when taken from the coal Tard.—Salt was then called as a witness, and stated that the business was his alone.—Allmark was then discharged, and Salt was fined 50s. and costs, or one month in default.
